POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Thu, 12 Nov 2026 22:34:30 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Not even old Andalusian heartlands can save Pedro Sánchez https://www.politico.eu/article/pedro-sanchez-uphill-battle-to-win-back-the-socialists-andalusian-heartland/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 20:45:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9317679 SEVILLE, Spain — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez officially launched his long-shot reelection bid in Seville on Thursday, appealing to Socialist loyalists in Andalusia, the southern region that for decades served as his party’s political heartland.

But even here, the center-left is now is on the ropes — in a stark sign of how improbable a Sánchez win now looks on Nov. 29.

Surrounded by Socialist supporters waving red party banners and Andalusian flags and shouting “¡Guapo!” — “Handsome!” — the undaunted prime minister took the stage in Seville, dancing to the upbeat strains of a romantic pop song, chosen to underscore his progressive message of love in the face of the politics of hate.

“We’re here to vote, we’re here to win, we’re here to govern,” Sánchez told the adoring crowd, which had been shown videos of the prime minister reciting poems by Federico García Lorca, the celebrated Andalusian poet and playwright murdered by Francoist forces in 1936.

Sánchez’s decision to launch his campaign in Seville is laden with historic symbolism. For 36 years, the Socialists dominated Andalusian politics, controlling the regional government and many of the region’s biggest cities. 

That hold on power ended in 2018, after years of declining support and a string of corruption scandals paved the way for the center-right People’s Party to take control.

Since becoming regional president in 2019, Juanma Moreno has established himself as a steady, pragmatic leader, winning a landslide victory in 2022 and securing the most votes in snap elections earlier this year. His success in Andalusia has also elevated his profile nationally, making him one of the leading figures of the PP’s moderate wing.

Despite the PP’s consolidation of power in Andalusia, the Socialists are not ready to relinquish their claim on the region. Francisco Toscano, a Socialist candidate for congress in Seville, told POLITICO the party still considered Andalusia to be its bastion.

“This is an eminently progressive region, and one whose voters believe in progressive government,” he said.

Electorally, he added, Andalusia is crucial to the Socialists’ grander ambitions. “This is the most populous autonomous community in Spain, so its weight at the national level is very important,” he continued, noting that the region elects the largest number of lawmakers to the parliament in Madrid, making up 60 of the 350 seats.

But while Sánchez’s campaign launch struck an optimistic note about the prospect of an Andalusian comeback, the latest polling suggests the Socialists could suffer disastrous results across the region.

According to the latest GAD3 poll, the center-right People’s Party is ahead of the Socialists in most Andalusian provinces — including Seville, where Sánchez’s party has never previously lost in a general election.

A rout in Andalusia would be more than a regional setback for Sánchez. It would further narrow his slim path to reelection, making a fresh national mandate look all the more out of reach.

Reversal of fortune

The Socialists’ decline in Andalusia is, in many ways, a consequence of their own success.

When the party first came to power in the region in 1982, Andalusia was one of Spain’s poorest areas. But under leaders such as Manuel Chaves — who ruled the region for 19 years — it underwent a profound transformation.

Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, Socialist regional governments used EU structural funds to spur economic development, funding infrastructure projects such as the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway.

Between 1982 and 1996, Socialist Prime Minister Felipe González — a proud native son on Seville — championed the region from Madrid, helping secure major investments and backing landmark events such as the Expo ’92 World’s Fair, which brought a fresh wave of investment to Andalusia.

But as regional living standards improved, voters’ expectations rose too — and the party increasingly struggled to meet them.

“There was a paradox of satisfaction,” said Ángel Cazorla, a political scientist at the University of Granada. “Although Andalusians felt the Socialists had overseen decades of progress, and personally felt their lives had improved, the great recession exposed how much remained unfinished or unresolved.” 

By 2018, frustration over persistent problems such as unemployment and strained public services, and corruption cases involving high-ranking regional grandees, ultimately led to the Socialists’ ouster.

Cazorla said the two deadly train accidents that rocked Spain this year, both of which occurred on the iconic Madrid-Seville rail line, were emblematic of the party’s decline. 

“In addition to the human toll, we can list Curro as a victim of these tragedies,” he said, referring to the colorful cartoon bird that served as the mascot of the 1992 Seville World’s Fair and which many Andalusians associate with the prosperity of the Socialist era.

“The deadly accidents are in a lot of ways representative of a social-democratic project that gradually ran out of steam, and that successive governments have failed to look after what had been achieved not only with infrastructure, but public goods and overall quality of life,” he added.

The generational gap

Socialist candidate Toscano is not blind to the reasons the Socialists have lost ground. 

After decades in power, he acknowledged, the party had faced growing pressure from the right, corruption scandals and a failure to adapt its message to changing living standards. “We had shortcomings in our management in recent years,” he said, while arguing the Socialists had nonetheless remained electorally competitive in parts of the region.

Cazorla argued the party’s difficulties go beyond its record in government: It also faces a generational problem. Younger electors who grew up in an already-transformed Andalusia feel little identification with the Socialists or with a regional leadership associated with the discredited administrations of the past. 

“A young left-wing voter is paying attention to a different message — one the old guard is incapable of projecting,” he said, adding Adelante Andalucía, a regionalist party that advocates in favor of greater self-government and left-wing policies, is more likely to seduce local electors.

Toscano, however, remained hopeful that Andalusian voters would turn out for the Socialists in an election he frames as a choice between Sánchez’s progressive agenda and the global conservative wave. 

“We’ve seen public services deteriorate under Giorgia Meloni in Italy, and Javier Milei wielding his ‘chainsaw’ to dismantle Argentina’s welfare state,” he said. “In this election, Spaniards must choose whether to remain a country that continues to make social progress or follow the path of regression we are seeing elsewhere.”

]]> en Climate science says 1.5C is dead. No one wants to bury it.  https://www.politico.eu/article/climate-science-1-5c-target-global-warming-dead/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 18:27:58 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9315162 ANTALYA, Turkey — “Anything is possible if you believe,” croons Turkish pop megastar Tarkan in his theme song for this year’s global COP31 climate conference.

Attendees appear to have taken his words to heart.

The Antalya summit marks the first climate talks since the United Nations told the world global warming would soon exceed 1.5C, effectively burying the totemic Paris Agreement target that has steered COP negotiations for more than a decade.

Yet leaders here are straining to keep the goal on life support.

“We are on course to overshoot the 1.5 degree target, and every fraction of a degree matters. So we must double down,” said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her speech to fellow leaders on Wednesday.

“Let’s show that the fight for 1.5C is not over,” Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands told leaders.

Even before the talks began, Danish Climate Minister Samira Nawa told POLITICO her country’s priority at COP31 was “to push for keeping the 1.5C target in the heart of global climate ambitions.”

Other leaders and ministers, reviving slogans from COPs past, have exhorted their colleagues to “keep 1.5 alive” or ensure the target remains “within reach.”

But scientists say that dream is over.

The U.N. last month said that, even if countries dramatically slash planet-warming emissions starting right now, the best outcome would be a rise in global temperatures of 1.8 degrees. If they also deploy vast amounts of carbon removal tech to clean up the atmosphere, there’s a chance of getting back to 1.5 degrees after surpassing it — in theory.

In reality, though, greenhouse gas emissions are still rising and the carbon-hoovering technologies needed to achieve that reversal are unproven at scale.

The risk

The collective ambition of national climate plans, already insufficient before the U.N.’s announcement, is even weaker than projected last year. Countries that have been among the strongest proponents of meeting the 1.5-degree target are watering down efforts to achieve it.

But at the same time, many countries (and climate scientists) fear that publicly dumping the rhetoric around 1.5C will open the door to weakening global ambitions even further. Highlighting other possible targets, such as the 1.8C mentioned by the U.N., would be a “slippery slope,” warned one European climate negotiator.

“I do not support the political messaging of keeping 1.5C alive — but on the other hand, I don’t want to lose it,” said Johan Rockström, a leading climate scientist and director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.

“Politicians, when they say that, may naively think that we somehow still are on this linear, incremental journey that can simply take us to safety, which is not the case,” he added. “On the other hand, if we scientifically criticize it, the risk is that they do indeed say: ‘OK, let’s just drop it and aim for 2 degrees instead,’ which would be a big mistake.”

Beyond symbolism

For island nations already losing land and livelihoods to rising oceans, the 1.5 degree target is not merely symbolic. It represents their very survival.

“Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over,” said Heine, the Marshall Islands president. “Overshoot means waves eating away our shores, flooding that destroys towns, schools, hospitals. It destroys our land and ocean.”

The temperature target was not chosen arbitrarily. It represents the level of warming scientists say the planet can endure before the heat trapped in the atmosphere unleashes exponentially greater dangers.

In the Paris accord, countries vowed to limit warming to below 2 degrees and “ideally” 1.5 degrees. The second target has become so dominant that the International Court of Justice last year declared it the primary goal.

A group of developed and highly vulnerable nations, known as the High Ambition Coalition, have called for a credible response to the overshoot as one key COP31 outcome.

“There is no way we can lose that anchor, out of our moral responsibility toward the people who have contributed the least and are the most impacted,” said Christiana Figueres, who headed the U.N. climate body when the Paris Agreement was adopted.

Words vs. action

But promises have not aligned with reality.

“Leaders, and in particular those from developed countries, cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5 degrees,” U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres told world leaders in his opening speech on Wednesday.

Yet immediately after his speech, leaders did just that.

Australia, COP31 co-hosts with Turkey, is expanding investments in coal and natural gas, even as its Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen urges leaders in Antalya to act with “urgency, solidarity and resolve.”

“With every minute that we fail to achieve the targets set out in the Paris Agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. Two days earlier, he had celebrated the discovery of two new oil fields.

“The science is clear. Breaching 1.5 isn’t where we down tools and give up,” Katie White, the U.K.’s climate minister, said in response to the U.N. findings. White promised COP31 was the place to double down on action — but a day later, her own department approved a major natural gas project in the North Sea.

Meanwhile the United States, the largest polluter in world history, has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement and is no longer part of COP talks. Donald Trump’s abandonment of efforts to address global warming has left a large gap in the world’s collective efforts to cut emissions.

There’s always next year

Tina Stege, the Marshall Islands’ climate envoy, acknowledged the difficulty of the challenge. But she was unbending.

“That’s not a reason to not do everything that we absolutely can,” she told reporters. “Every country that showed up at this talk to do the work needs to do that work and more.”

Doing more means ramping up clean electrification and alternative fuels, say experts.

It also means dramatically curbing short-term climate pollutants, such as methane. That’s emerging as a possible response to the overshoot declaration in the final agreement from this year’s negotiations, according to the European diplomat cited above.

“If we cut methane by nearly half by 2030, we could avoid almost 0.3 degrees of warming by the 2040s and save 250,000 lives every year,” said Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, on Wednesday. “This buys us the time to get back to the 1.5 degrees.”

The politics are tricky. Even as technological advances have allowed for better detection of the potent pollutant, the U.S. and Europe have weakened regulations aimed at curbing methane emissions.

Mottley was adamant nonetheless that flagging global ambitions were no reason to give up.

“I call for a global movement: 1.5 billion voices for 1.5 degrees,” she said. “We need to do this before we meet at COP32 next year. … Make 1.5 impossible to ignore on the planet Earth.”

]]> en De grandes villes européennes demandent à l’UE d’interdire les filtres des cigarettes https://www.politico.eu/article/de-grandes-villes-europeennes-demandent-a-lue-dinterdire-les-filtres-des-cigarettes/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:20:22 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9315597 BRUXELLES — De grandes villes européennes font pression pour que l’UE interdise la vente de filtres pour cigarettes. Elles dénoncent des embouts en plastique n’ayant aucun avantage en matière de santé et représentant la principale source de déchets urbains.

Bruxelles, Munich, Dublin et Gênes font partie des municipalités qui ont rejoint la campagne “No (Plastic) Filter”, une initiative soutenue par la mairie de La Haye et par le gouvernement néerlandais, ainsi que par d’autres villes, mais aussi des autorités chargées de la gestion de l’eau et des associations écologistes.

Elles affirment que le principe inscrit dans le droit européen de “responsabilité élargie du producteur” — des règles obligeant les fabricants de tabac à prendre en charge les coûts de gestion des déchets — n’a pas permis de réduire la pollution causée par les filtres des cigarettes et qu’une interdiction totale s’impose.

“Les mégots de cigarette représentent pas moins de 30% de tous les détritus dans la ville de Bruxelles. Non seulement ces déchets dégradent notre paysage urbain, mais leur ramassage fait peser une charge extraordinaire sur nos équipes de nettoyage”, a pointé Anas Ben Abdelmoumen, conseiller municipal chargé de la propreté publique, auprès de POLITICO.

Plusieurs autres villes de Belgique, d’Allemagne, de Tchéquie, de Hongrie et de Lituanie ont également rejoint cette campagne, qui intervient alors que l’Union européenne procède à la révision de deux textes législatifs majeurs susceptibles d’aboutir à l’interdiction des filtres des cigarettes — ou du moins du plastique qu’ils contiennent.

La révision de la directive sur les produits du tabac par la Commission européenne est l’occasion d’interdire les filtres des cigarettes, estiment les membres de la campagne. S’ils échouent par ce biais, ils pourraient se rabattre sur la révision à venir de la directive sur les plastiques à usage unique pour interdire le plastique dans les filtres.

L’Organisation mondiale de la Santé est elle aussi en faveur de l’interdiction ou de la suppression progressive des filtres, affirmant qu’ils ne présentent aucun avantage pour la santé.

“Le filtre de cigarette est l’objet le plus souvent jeté dans l’espace public, il contient du plastique, il est à l’origine d’une pollution environnementale toxique et engendre des coûts considérables pour les collectivités locales et la société. De plus, le filtre ne rend pas le tabagisme moins nocif”, a argumenté Karl Beerenfenger, responsable de la campagne et membre de l’ONG néerlandaise Fair Resource Foundation.

“C’est un produit trompeur, l’une des plus grandes escroqueries de l’histoire récente. Le filtre de cigarette n’aurait jamais dû être mis sur le marché.”

L’industrie du tabac affirme toutefois que les filtres ont bel et bien une utilité sur le plan sanitaire.

“Il n’existe pas de cigarette sans danger, avec ou sans filtre”, a énoncé Nathan Jones, responsable de la stratégie réglementaire européenne chez British American Tobacco. “Cependant, des études montrent que les filtres contribuent à réduire l’exposition à certaines substances toxiques et nous aident à respecter la législation européenne régissant les émissions des cigarettes. S’il existait une alternative viable et déployable à grande échelle, nous l’utiliserions, mais il n’y en a pas.”

Le pollueur par excellence

A La Haye, les coûts liés au nettoyage des mégots de cigarette sont estimés à environ 2 millions d’euros par an, selon la maire adjointe de la ville, Isabelle Broeders.

“De notre point de vue, l’évaluation de la directive sur les produits du tabac représente une occasion importante d’[interdire les filtres des cigarettes]. Nous plaidons en faveur d’une interdiction de tous les filtres des cigarettes, quel que soit le matériau utilisé”, a détaillé Isabelle Broeders à POLITICO.

La plupart des filtres des cigarettes sont fabriqués à partir d’acétate de cellulose, un type de plastique d’origine végétale qui se décompose difficilement. Il existe des alternatives biodégradables, mais elles ne sont pas largement utilisées. Les fabricants ont fait pression pour que l’acétate de cellulose soit classé comme un produit durable et biodégradable, et qu’il soit exempté de la directive sur les plastiques à usage unique.

Le lobby Tobacco Europe s’est opposé à l’éventualité d’une restriction des filtres en plastique par la Commission, espérant que l’UE se concentre plutôt sur “la sensibilisation, l’application effective des règles contre les déchets sauvages et la mise en œuvre proportionnée de la REP [responsabilité élargie du producteur], tout en favorisant l’innovation afin de proposer des alternatives viables à terme”.

Mais Bruxelles et La Haye sont toutes deux convaincues que le simple fait d’interdire le plastique présent à l’intérieur du filtre ne suffirait pas.

“Autoriser des alternatives au plastique crée une faille dangereuse : les fabricants pourraient introduire de nouveaux matériaux qui échappent aux définitions techniques du plastique, tout en restant pratiquement aussi nocifs, persistants dans l’environnement et préjudiciables à la propreté publique”, a soulevé Anas Ben Abdelmoumen.

Le gouvernement néerlandais, quant à lui, affirme qu’il se concentre sur les plastiques présents dans les filtres des cigarettes dans le cadre de la révision de la directive sur les plastiques à usage unique. “Si cette approche s’avérait infructueuse, cet objectif pourrait également être atteint par le biais de la [directive sur les produits du tabac]”, a indiqué un porte-parole à POLITICO.

Selon Yogi Hendlin, philosophe de l’environnement et chercheur en santé publique à l’université Erasmus de Rotterdam, les filtres constituent une “prothèse fixée à l’extrémité de la cigarette” dont les gens pensent qu’elle retient “les éléments les plus nocifs de la fumée”.

“Mais le filtre en lui-même n’apporte aucun bénéfice pour la santé”, a-t-il affirmé, et il a même été démontré qu’il augmentait le risque de cancer du poumon. “Il ne filtre aucune des substances cancérigènes, et ne fait guère mieux en matière de filtration. Il s’agit essentiellement d’un changement de couleur purement esthétique qui trompe votre esprit en lui faisant croire que vous êtes plus en sécurité que vous ne l’êtes réellement.”

Yogi Hendlin a évoqué une affaire judiciaire américaine marquante de 2006, dans laquelle il avait été établi que les fabricants de tabac avaient induit les fumeurs en erreur en commercialisant des cigarettes “light” et “à faible teneur en goudron” comme des produits moins nocifs.

]]> fr ‘Blind spot’ no longer: Austria targets Russian espionage with new law https://www.politico.eu/article/austria-targets-russian-espionage-with-new-legislation/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 16:26:55 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9315270 Vienna has long had a reputation for being a nest of spies, but Austria is stepping up its crackdown on espionage.

“Austria will no longer be a blind spot in Europe’s security,” Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger told POLITICO on Thursday, after the government approved draft legislation to strengthen its espionage laws on Wednesday.

“Foreign intelligence services are operating increasingly aggressively in Austria,” the country’s chancellor, Christian Stocker, added. “We are putting a stop to this by tightening our laws. In doing so, we are also helping to protect our European partners and the many international organizations based in Austria.”

While the new legislation targets espionage in general, it is part of the ministry’s broader shift in policy toward Russia, according to an internal document seen by POLITICO.

Under Austria’s current Criminal Code, operating or supporting a clandestine intelligence service is punishable if it harms Austrian interests. But espionage targeting other countries or international organizations is not covered in the same way, a loophole the government now wants to close.

The proposed legislation would introduce prison sentences of up to five years for espionage targeting EU institutions or international organizations with headquarters or offices in Austria, such as the United Nations, the OSCE and the International Atomic Energy Agency. The maximum sentence for espionage against Austria itself would increase from five to 10 years.

Austria pressured Russia earlier this year to dismantle satellite installations on its diplomatic properties in Vienna over concerns they could be used for espionage. At least three installations have since been removed. The country has expelled eight Russian diplomats since March 2025 for suspected espionage.

“Austria’s lax approach to spies is now firmly a thing of the past. Vienna remains a place for dialogue, but will no longer be a hub for espionage,” Meinl-Reisinger added, acknowledging that Vienna has long been known as a hotbed of spying.

Austria’s neutrality and its status as a non-NATO member have contributed to that reputation. During the Cold War, its proximity to the Iron Curtain made it a meeting point for intelligence services from East and West.

The draft law would also criminalize the recruitment of so-called disposable agents by foreign intelligence services and strengthen penalties for certain cybercrimes.

The legislation is expected to pass parliament next year and take effect in February 2027, according to a ministry spokesperson.

The move is part of a broader push to beef up Europe’s national security with several European countries revising national legislation and increasing powers of domestic intelligence agencies.

Antoaneta Roussi contributed to this report.

“Whether you speak to people from the Middle East, from sub-Saharan Africa, from Europe … all these fingers are pointed at President Trump and what he did in Iran. More so ironically — perversely — than Putin in Ukraine. President Trump has got Putin off the hook.”

The rhetoric on display in Turkey has not gone unnoticed in Washington, which has not sent a delegation to COP31. The U.S. withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change treaty that underpins COP talks will be completed early next year.

“President Trump is ensuring Iran can never have or use a nuclear weapon—a threat that would have a catastrophic impact on the entire world,” said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers. “The conflict in Iran has underscored the importance of having access to reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources.

“Nations around the world are now turning to the United States as both an example and a partner in pursuing common-sense energy dominance policies,” she argued.

Nonetheless, Khan’s criticisms of Trump — and a cautious optimism about post-2028 American climate policy — are echoed by other diplomats and campaigners in Turkey.

The U.S. midterms and even more importantly for most diplomats the reelection in Brazil of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva offer a “more positive vibe at COP31,” said founder of the E3G climate think tank Nick Mabey, “as countries see a move away from populism and the possibility of positive U.S. engagement on climate.”

“After Lula’s win and what we learned from the U.S. midterms,” agreed one European diplomat, “there’s a bit of a sense of tails up here now.”

“When the Americans and the Russians talk about this, it’s not just about security guarantees for Ukraine,” the Ukrainian president told leaders at the start of a summit in Dublin. “It’s more about some kind of new security framework between Europe and Russia.”

While he said it’s “very good that Europeans are now part of these talks,” they don’t speak directly to Russia so “we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of this negotiation.”

Two days of peace negotiations between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi ended on Wednesday without a breakthrough ― and without European officials joining the talks. EU governments continue to disagree over who would represent them. U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and  Jared Kushner, met the Russian leader on Thursday and will dash to Dublin to update Zelenskyy on Thursday evening.

Speaking on his way into the European Political Community summit in the Irish capital ― a gathering of 50 EU and non-EU leaders ― German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had received positive signals from the Abu Dhabi talks, but also stressed that Ukraine and Europe must be involved.

“I expect the Russian government and the Russian president to finally agree to these joint talks,” Merz said. “We will also discuss who, if necessary, will represent the European Union. But that is a matter we will discuss behind closed doors and not air publicly.”

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas struck a more skeptical tone, saying she had seen no goodwill from Moscow and insisted that a ceasefire must come before discussions on a peace agreement or Europe’s wider security architecture.

“Americans are representing American interests, Europeans are representing European interests,” she said, adding that EU treaties signal that European Council President António Costa and she should represent the bloc in any talks— a solution backed by Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal in an interview with POLITICO.

French President Emmanuel Macron said that Europe must first agree on its own peace proposals and vision for future European security before deciding who should represent it.

The substance of Europe’s negotiating position should determine the format of any talks, rather than the other way around, he told reporters on the way into the summit.

“Without Europeans there is no support for Ukraine, let’s be honest,” he said, arguing that U.S. involvement has declined. “There is some mediation, fine. But at the end of the day we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans. I have no doubt about it.” 

Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden backed Costa as the EU’s representative, while Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin called for a “clear, coherent leadership from the European Union at that table” warning that it remained unclear whether Russia was genuinely interested in peace.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev warned that Europe’s place in future negotiations was still not guaranteed, while his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš, expressed optimism that the bloc was moving closer to securing a seat at the table.

The issue is set to be discussed at Friday’s informal European Council following Meloni’s request. Costa agreed to make time for the discussion, on top of the original agenda focusing on AI.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:49:06 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Europe’s self-styled pacifists are helping Putin freeze Ukrainians in their homes https://euobserver.com/248586/europes-self-styled-pacifists-are-helping-putin-freeze-ukrainians-out/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248586 As Russia bombs Ukraine’s grid, Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria want to opt out of the next EU loan - money that actually also helps Ukrainian's civilians build back-up power and heating.]]> As it gets colder and darker, I think of my Ukrainian friends.

Russian bombing campaigns this year have targeted power and heating facilities, hoping to break morale and leave Ukrainians sitting in the cold and dark come winter. 

This past weekend alone, strikes on the high-voltage substations around the capital left 80 to 85 percent of Kyiv’s consumers without power. And it could get much worse. 

Last year, people were left without power and heating for much of the winter. It was often the elderly living in poorly insulated older homes at minus 20 degrees who suffered the most. 

The state has so far not succeeded in transitioning from the Soviet-era regulated system towards a more decentralised, more resilient energy system. But that doesn’t mean Ukrainian’s haven’t already started building parts of it themselves.

I visited the country in May to document how people were preparing for another harrowing winter by building bespoke back-up systems in their gardens, their sheds; on their roofs.  

Read more

War is driving Ukraine’s green energy build-out, but lack of money is holding it back

Across the country, small solar plants and battery storage systems went up to keep hospitals running and to make sure children did not have to sit in the dark in their schools’ bomb shelters for too long. 

New energy cooperatives have popped up all over Kyiv to pool scarce know-how in a country where the energy system still relies on a handful of giant Soviet-era power plants. 

We don’t talk about this enough at home, but a lot of these local and communal projects could not have been done without EU loans.

]]> EU Parliament asked to lift immunity of German far-right MEP accused of baseball‑bat attack on teen https://euobserver.com/248700/eu-parliament-asked-to-lift-immunity-of-german-far-right-mep-accused-of-baseballbat-attack-on-teen/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:42:53 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248700 The EU parliament was requested to waive a German far-right MEP’s immunity to allow his prosecution for drunk-driving and violently assaulting minors with a baseball bat.]]> The European Parliament has received a request to waive the immunity of a German far-right MEP to allow his prosecution for allegedly drink-driving and violently assaulting a minor with a baseball bat.

Parliament president Roberta Metsola confirmed having received a request to waive immunity of Arno Bausemer, of the Europe of Sovereign Nations hard-right group who is also the Alternative for Germany treasurer for Saxony-Anhalt, on Wednesday (11 November), so that east German region can prosecute him.

Bausemer is accused of attacking a 14-year-old with a baseball bat during the state’s election campaign in August.

He admitted to having “caught the teenager red-handed”, who he said was vandalising AfD campaign posters, and that he used a baseball bat.

“A suspected blunt weapon was allegedly used,” the Saxony-Anhalt State Criminal Police Office (LKA) confirmed.

A few days later, the MEP was stopped at a traffic control, where a blood sample reportedly showed an alcohol level of one gram per litre – double the allowed limit in Germany.

Parliamentary immunity is in place so that MEPs can “truly perform their mandate independently,” without fear of unjustified legal action, Wouter Wolfs, politics researcher at the KU Leuven, told EUobserver.

Read more

Neo-Nazi messages, links to Moscow, and Alice Weidel’s hypocrisy. 13 years of AfD emails have leaked

Parliamentary immunity guarantees MEPs will not be detained because of their opinions or how they voted, but also for offences they may be accused of. It protects politicians from legal battles designed to distract their attention from their parliamentary duties.

The only exception is when they were caught in the act – though what that means is sometimes disputed.

Currently, the immunity of 10 MEPs is under review in the European parliament, for offences ranging from a labour dispute to holocaust denial.

In some recent cases, the parliament kept MEPs immunity on “rather doubtful grounds,” Wolfs said, namely when their political allies protected them, but in essence, MEPs most often end up being put on trial.

The trouble with the immunity provision, German Green MEP Daniel Freund told EUobserver, is that it takes a long time to actually waive it, “undermining both parliament’s credibility and the principle that everyone is equal before the law.”

In most cases, the time between receiving a complaint by the parliament’s legal affairs committee – tasked with immunity waivers – and a plenary vote deciding on the matter is about five months, but up to a year in some cases.

Wolfs said he would expect the parliament to waive Bausemer’s immunity, so that the proceedings against him in his case may resume.

    ]]>         From pin-up calendars to the Istanbul Convention: Magyar’s U-turn, as Operation Purgatory reaches Orbán’s brother (Day 184 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/248651/from-pin-up-calendars-to-the-istanbul-convention-magyars-u-turn-as-operation-purgatory-reaches-orbans-brother-day-184-of-the-tisza-government/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 16:48:36 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248651 Hungary’s political landscape is shifting dramatically as the new Tisza government challenges Viktor Orbán’s 16-year legacy. With Orbán’s brother facing detention, Fidesz support plunging to historic lows and corruption investigations gaining public backing, the country is entering a new political chapter. The government has also announced ambitious gender-equality measures, including stronger protections against domestic violence, improved reproductive rights and plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention.]]> The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:

    • Orbán’s brother on a leash
    • Péter Magyar and women
    • The new head of state takes on the asset‑protection law
    • Fidesz is in freefall – no one knows where it will stop
    • Even Fidesz voters consider uncovering corruption cases important

    Áron Orbán on a leash

    For 16 years it had been utterly unthinkable that an official measure could reach all the way into former prime minister Viktor Orbán’s family. Now this has happened. On Monday (9 November), Áron Orbán, the brother of the former prime minister, was taken into custody. And not only was he detained, he was later also remanded in pre‑trial detention for one month due to the risk of tampering with evidence.

    Áron Orbán’s case, which has been taken over by the National Office for Asset Recovery and Asset Protection set up by the new government, is rather convoluted. Put simply, it concerns a group which, citing its political connections, told companies and entrepreneurs engaged in recruiting foreign labour that if they arranged residence permits through them, they would in any case obtain the necessary visas.

    In the case, an investigation was launched on suspicion of influence peddling and other criminal offences, but it did not move forward until the elections; afterwards, however, several arrests were made.

    This offers an intriguing parallel with current events in Serbia: there, the authorities set about the dirty work almost immediately after former president Aleksandar Vučić’s fall and arrested major players – clearly everything had long been prepared there as well, only those in power had not allowed the wheels of justice to turn.

    Read more

    After students voted out Vučić, can Serbia’s uprising against ‘evil’ change how the state really works?

    According to the Budapest Prosecutor’s Office, over several months in 2024 Áron Orbán and his three associates helped Vietnamese citizens get to Western Europe via Hungary.

    According to the allegations, they assisted in visa procedures at Hungarian consular posts, for which they charged a so‑called recruitment fee per person and then shared the proceeds. Based on the authorities’ information, they may have helped more than one hundred Vietnamese nationals.

    Péter Magyar and women

    At the start of the week, it looked like prime minister Péter Magyar was heading for a difficult week in office.

    On Monday, he addressed parliament about his government’s first six months, but attention quickly shifted to a controversy over communist-era secret police records. Lists published from the archives wrongly identified 164 people, including Fidesz politician Sándor Lezsák, as former agents, when they had actually been victims of surveillance.

    Magyar apologised but argued that the archives are controlled by parliament, not his government. However, since making these records public was a long-promised part of his political agenda, he should take responsibility for the mistake rather than shift the blame.

    On top of that, Magyar also bungled the latest episode of his ongoing political communication soap opera, called Absolute Movie Theater. On Sunday, in his video he showed viewers the lesser‑known parts of the Parliament building, where calendars featuring naked women could be seen on the wall of a basement maintenance workshop.

    Our former colleague Veronika Munk, editor‑in‑chief of 444.hu, directly confronted the issue in an opinion piece, sharply criticising the video, the objectification of women’s bodies and the conspiratorial, primitive machismo.

    The Hungarian prime minister, a prolific Facebook commenter, could not resist weighing in. Commenting under the 444 article, he mocked Munk’s view that crude, breast-focused images are among the most degrading ways women are portrayed in the media. Clearly, he did not agree.

    The situation was further aggravated by the fact that on Wednesday the parliamentary committee investigating abuses in the enforcement system under the previous regime – the Völner–Schadl case – heard Judit Varga, Péter Magyar’s ex‑wife and Viktor Orbán’s former justice minister.

    The former minister did not say much that was new about the case itself, stating that she had had no opportunity to “expose” her former state secretary, Pál Völner, who was up to his neck in the affair. She spoke much more, however, about her ex‑husband, even though this was not really relevant to the subject.

    But Magyar’s superpower is that he can always turn things around. And on Thursday morning (12 November), he did just that. In a video he announced that, after many months of work, a comprehensive social and criminal‑law package would be adopted to protect victims of domestic violence and abused women.

    According to Magyar’s announcement, the package contains a large number of very important commitments.

    • They would tighten restraining‑order rules, so that after a request for help the abuser could not approach the victim, for example, at her home or workplace.
    • They would make the misuse of intimate recordings a standalone criminal offence.
    • They would clearly enshrine the requirement of voluntary consent for sexual acts.
    • They would ensure special treatment for victims of relationship violence in criminal proceedings.
    • They would amend the heartbeat decree. Before terminating a pregnancy, after receiving medical information, the woman concerned could decide for herself whether she wants the signs of the foetus’s vital functions to be shown to her.
    • They would abolish the prescription requirement for the morning‑after pill, so emergency contraception would be available without a prescription.
    • They would launch measures against period poverty, so that those for whom buying basic hygiene products is a financial burden can also obtain them.
    • They would strengthen support for pregnant women.
    • The government will initiate the ratification of the Istanbul Convention. The convention lays down obligations for preventing violence against women and domestic violence, protecting victims and prosecuting perpetrators.

    Read more

    Is Europe succeeding in combatting violence against women?

    Neither the amendment of the heartbeat decree nor the ratification of the Istanbul Convention featured in Tisza’s election programme.

    The new head of state is not a signing machine

    Hungary’s new president, András Baka, has shown that he will not automatically approve everything put before him. This week, he refused to sign a government-backed law that could give the state greater influence over investment funds and weaken protections for minority shareholders.

    Baka argued that the law was too broad, could affect existing funds with no state involvement, and offered insufficient protection to smaller investors. He also criticised the fact that it was passed just 26 hours after being introduced, without proper consultation, warning that such unpredictable interventions could undermine investor confidence. He has referred the legislation to the Constitutional Court for review.

    His decision marks a significant departure from the practice of his predecessors, who rarely challenged laws important to the government. For the first time in years, Hungary has a president willing to use his office to question legislation on substantive grounds – a welcome sign for the country’s democracy.

    Read more

    Hungary’s communist secret‑police files go online – and a Fidesz MP is named by mistake (Day 178 of the Tisza government)

    Fidesz is in freefall – no one knows where it will stop

    Meanwhile, former PM Viktor Orbán and his circle are still not in very good shape. Medián, the polling agency that predicted the election results most accurately, published a new survey at the beginning of the week, according to which Fidesz’s support has plummeted – while Tisza’s has risen.

    The voters clearly do not feel that “Tisza‑style despotism” is raging, as Fidesz politicians keep repeating like a mantra. In the total population, 55 percent would currently vote for the governing party, while Fidesz has fallen to 16 percent. This is a low not seen for several decades; they were last this weak in the mid‑1990s.

    With such a vote share, Tisza would win more than 160 seats in parliament if elections were held now.     Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    Find the full transcript below:

    Ukraine’s war effort depends heavily on two American tools: Starlink and Starshield. Both belong to Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and both can be switched off. Europe says it wants to reduce that dependence.

    Is it possible, and why is Europe so far behind? Starlink is SpaceX’s satellite internet service. It’s sold to the general public, to companies and to armies. It relies on a constellation of around 10,000 satellites in low orbit, which makes it possible to get a connection almost anywhere on Earth.

    Starshield is the version designed for governments and militaries. It uses the same technology, but with dedicated satellites and dedicated encryption. In other words, it’s more secure.

    Read more

    Russia faces a strategic crisis and record losses, but thanks to Trump it sees things positively (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,713)

    The problem is that its use completely depends on the goodwill of Elon Musk. But also on the US government. Starshield is a government system, and it’s Washington that actually makes it available to Ukraine.

    This has already led to some awkward situations. A few weeks ago, Ukraine noticed that the speed of its drones had been throttled overnight. The explanation was clear: it was an American move. The issue has since been resolved, but it illustrates a real unease.

    So how did Ukraine end up in this position? At the start of the war, the country’s cable-based internet infrastructure was damaged. On the battlefield, the army now uses SpaceX terminals to receive internet signal, because they’re small and very practical.

    And that is exactly what Europeans don’t offer. Most European satellites are in high orbit. They cover very large areas, but they have two drawbacks in wartime. Because they are further away, the delay in transmission is longer. Second, the equipment needed to receive the signal is much bulkier, so it is not suited to the front line.

    Elon Musk made a very strategic choice: putting tens of thousands of satellites in low orbit.  It’s much cheaper, and much easier to operate. Now could Europeans compete on this market?

    The closest European equivalent, on a smaller scale, is the OneWeb constellation, run by the French company Eutelsat. Eutelsat was originally a European intergovernmental organisation. But it was dismantled and its activity has been taken over by a company.

    The French state is still its largest shareholder, with around a third of the shares. The United Kingdom and an Indian group also hold stakes.

    Through OneWeb, Eutelsat has around 680 satellites, in both low and high orbit. The company says it could replace Starlink in the medium term, meaning sometime in the 2030s.

    It plans to reinforce its fleet with several hundred new satellites. But most of them will actually replace older ones. So it’s not a big increase, compared with Starlink.

    Read more

    Russia’s fake war maps at Abu Dhabi peace talks aren’t fooling anyone (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,721)

    There is also another project designed to secure European connections. It’s called IRIS². This one is a European project, carried out by several companies, including Eutelsat. The EU is its main customer. Unlike OneWeb, it’s not a commercial venture. But both share the same goal: reducing dependence on Starlink.

    The ambition is a constellation of at least 348 satellites by 2030, with deployment starting in 2029. So again, fewer than a thousand. That’s still far from Starlink.

    But here, it’s worth saying that satellites in low orbit are much cheaper to put in place, which also explains the sheer volume SpaceX has been able to launch in recent years.

    With far fewer satellites, but in higher orbit, Europeans can also cover the whole planet. It’s just that the system isn’t as flexible.

    Finally, is money part of the explanation? Yes, of course. The United States spends around six times more on its space programmes, civil and military, than Europeans do.

    There’s also another factor that helps SpaceX deploy thousands of satellites at low cost: it has its own launcher, the Falcon 9.

    Eutelsat, on the other hand, has to buy launches from third parties. So it’s much more expensive, and it doesn’t control the pace at which it can put satellites into orbit.

    Before wrapping up, a quick word about China, another big actor. It’s quite new in the space industry, and it’s not really spending huge amounts of money for the moment. But it’s worth keeping an eye on Beijing on this front too.

    ]]>         Consumers pay the price for online manipulation, and the EU Digital Fairness Act can put a stop to it https://euobserver.com/247929/consumers-pay-the-price-for-online-manipulation-and-the-eu-digital-fairness-act-can-put-a-stop-to-it/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:35:02 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247929 The EU's Digital Fairness Act (DFA) is one of the few initiatives of this legislative term through which Europe can improve people's lives by strengthening their consumer rights and helping them save money, write the Socialists & Democrats.]]> Think about the last thing you did before going to sleep, and the first thing you did when you woke up. Look around you on the bus or the metro. We are hooked on our devices and the online services behind them.

    That is not a personal failing. It is by design, part of a business model.

    Digital products that we use daily – whether apps, social media platforms or online marketplaces – make their profits by exploiting our attention, our mental health and our vulnerabilities.

    Feeds that never end, subscriptions that are near impossible to cancel, and fake countdowns that push us to click and buy on impulse are no accident. They are deliberate design features with a direct impact on our wellbeing and our wallets.

    Today, the European Commission is presenting the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) as a proposal to fight these and other unfair online practices.

    It is one of the few initiatives of this legislative term through which Europe can improve people’s lives by strengthening their consumer rights and helping them save money.

    Unfair commercial practices are estimated to cost European consumers close to €8bn a year. Whether or not the DFA will become a game changer in the fight against addictive and manipulative design will depend on the ambition the EU shows.

    Read more

    Digital Fairness Act: EU cracks down on influencer ads and manipulative app design

    Despite the clear need for digital fairness, new rules will face opposition from some quarters, notably US Big Tech.

    It runs against their push to deregulate under the guise of “simplification”, and it could risk triggering transatlantic retaliation from the US administration.

    Some may also argue that we already have rules: the Digital Services Act (DSA), they will say, already tackles dark patterns and addictive design. It does not, at least not fully, not for all consumers and not across all digital spaces.

    We need to remember that 97 percent of the most popular apps and websites still use them, so the rules currently in place have not put an end to this online manipulation.

    Concrete demands

    As Socialists & Democrats, we have a clear vision of what a strong DFA can deliver for consumers. Our concrete demands are:

    Ban dark patterns. Things like subscription traps, long click paths to cancel, free trials that turn into paid plans without warning, forced registration, fake other people are viewing this alerts, and items that appear in your basket at checkout should all be prohibited outright.

    Restrict addictive design for all consumers. Features such as endless scrolling should be restricted for everyone, not only children. The bill recently proposed in the Netherlands can serve as an inspiration for Europe.

    Make influencers and the money behind them accountable. Influencers who promote illegal or fraudulent products should be held personally responsible. Commercial deals must be disclosed clearly, not hidden as “#ad” at the end of a hundred hashtags. Those paying influencers also need to be held to account. The products they promote can damage people’s health as well as their finances.

    Put an end to manipulative pricing. Imagine queuing for an ice cream on a sunny Saturday, only to find that it now costs €6 instead of the €3.50 you paid last week – just because it’s hotter and busier. This is unfair pricing, and we want it to be banned in transport, live entertainment, culture and sport. Concerts and matches should not only be for the rich. A car ride should cost the same regardless of your background, your data or your phone’s battery level. People want transparency, but they also want limits, especially in emergency situations, when they are most vulnerable and have no control over the circumstances. 

    Stop gambling-like features in games. Most gamers are adults, not children. Loot boxes and pay-to-win mechanisms should be prohibited so that everyone can play without being manipulated or trapped. This is also a matter of affordability: consumers should not feel forced to buy more than they want to.

    The principle is simple: fairness and safety, by design and by default, should be the rule for every company, whether it runs an app, a social network or an online marketplace. This would also protect the many honest businesses that are undercut today by competitors willing to manipulate their customers.

    At the end of the day, this is also about who holds power online.

    Holding Big Tech companies accountable for how their services shape our behaviour, through surveillance-based ads, harmful content and addictive design, is part of regaining Europe’s digital sovereignty.

    The EU Commission has the evidence, the mandate and our backing. The EU Kids Act, was an important step forward in protecting minors online. Let’s see if Ursula von der Leyen’s executive now shows the same determination to ensure a safer online space for everyone, children and adults alike.

    We will assess the DFA by one test: will it make people’s lives online safer, fairer and more affordable? Consumers should not have to wait any longer to be protected online.

    Reining in Big Tech is a top priority for us, and we’ll be fighting to make sure this legislation protects us all online.

That’s what the latest EU Climate Action Progress Report and the Carbon Market Report, published on Monday, show. Yet, progress is still needed to achieve the 2030 objectives.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    EU greenhouse gas emissions continue to fall, and clean technologies are expanding. That’s what the latest EU Climate Action Progress Report and the Carbon Market Report, published on Monday, show. Yet, progress is still needed to achieve the 2030 objectives. 

    How are EU countries performing in reducing their carbon footprint? By the end of this decade, the EU should have cut its emissions by at least 55 percent compared with 1990 levels. By 2050, it should be climate neutral. Is it on the right track?

    The EU is reducing its emissions, but at a slower pace than needed. In other words, efforts will have to accelerate in the second half of the decade, starting now.

    Read more

    EU states back one-year methane delay, but leave door open for more

    Last year, in 2025, greenhouse gas emissions fell by 1.6 percent compared with the previous year.

    The report distinguishes between two types of emissions: those covered by the carbon market, the ETS, and the rest.

    Emissions covered by the carbon market tend to fall a bit faster, by 2 percent exactly. We are talking about sectors such as electricity production, refineries, metals, aviation and maritime transport. They fall faster because companies have to pay for every tonne of carbon they emit. That’s the polluter pays principle. 

    Now, 1.6 percent, 2 percent: that’s not much compared with the climate emergency. 

    On Monday, the Global Carbon Project released a study showing that global greenhouse gas emissions decreased last year for the first time since 2020. The decrease was 0.4 percent, so not huge, and the authors warned it was far from enough to counter climate change. The emissions peak is still not in sight.

    The conclusion is: we need to accelerate that transition.

    In the EU, which countries are lagging? Nine member states are not making sufficient progress towards their 2030 targets, according to the commission’s report. They are Austria, Croatia, Cyprus, Germany, Italy, Ireland, Lithuania, Malta and Sweden.

    Read more

    From India to Africa, renewables race ahead but Europe is lagging, IEA report shows

    What is holding them back? Well, each country has its specificity. In Italy, the energy mix is still very much dominated by gas. In Sweden, rising energy demand, looser climate policies and fewer carbon sinks undermine the climate objectives. Some countries struggle to solve problems with land use, while others are not switching to renewables fast enough.

    In any case, the commission will ask these nine countries to submit a corrective action plan to speed up emission-reduction measures and investments.

    Another EU plan to accelerate the transition is to extend the carbon market to road transport, heating and small industry, which have so far been exempt. This should help reduce pollution. But it was supposed to start next year, and member states have already delayed it by a year.

    ]]>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/12/starbucks-workers-campus-rally-contract-talks</link>
      <description><p>Rallies will take place on more than US 40 campuses as workers seeking better pay and conditions decry stalled talks</p><p>Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are planning rallies at <a href="https://starbucksworkersunited.controlshift.app/events?link_id=2&amp;can_id=debd8d2ad19f005d15f9bbdff314d42a&amp;source=email-nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;email_referrer=email_3490793&amp;email_subject=nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;&amp;">over 40 college campuses</a> across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United <a href="https://www.boycottstarbucks.net/">boycott campaign</a> as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.</p><p>Starbucks Workers United is <a href="https://sbworkersunited.org/what-were-fighting-for-updates-on-contract-bargaining/">seeking</a> better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store. It has called on the public to <a href="https://www.boycottstarbucks.net/">boycott</a> Starbucks until its first contract is reached.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/12/starbucks-workers-campus-rally-contract-talks">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/12/home-sales-october-low</link>
      <description><p>Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high</p><p>US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by record-high <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/mortgage-rates">mortgage rates</a> and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.</p><p>Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/12/home-sales-october-low">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’</p><p>Is this an opportunity for a new America? The project includes rolling back <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire.       <description><p>Trump-appointed judge Jeffrey T Kuntz partially denies British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over edit</p><p>Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case.       <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>
