<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 12 Nov 2026 23:58:12 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Meath construction firm obtains enforcement orders for €9.8m arbitration award against developer]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/construction-firm-granted-orders-for-enforcement-of-98m-arbitration-award-against-developer/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/construction-firm-granted-orders-for-enforcement-of-98m-arbitration-award-against-developer/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 16:41:05 +0000A Co Meath construction firm has obtained court orders providing for the enforcement of a €9.8 million arbitration award against a company linked to several major Dublin developers.

High Court president Judge David Barnville this week granted the orders to Midland Construction & Engineering Ltd, after an arbitrator in February found developer Baystreet had unlawfully terminated a contract between the two firms in 2024, according to court documents.

Developers John McKeon, Liam McSharry and Brian Kennedy are directors of Baystreet, which entered voluntary liquidation in September 2025.

Separate from the arbitration enforcement proceedings, Midland has issued proceedings against the Baystreet directors and shareholders. The case is due to come before the Commercial Court, the High Court’s big business division.

In written evidence, Midland director Thomas Stronge said his firm was engaged by Baystreet in 2022 to build 44 apartments at the developer’s project at Ashbrook in Clontarf, Dublin. The sum agreed for the works was some €9.6 million, later rising to €10.8 million, Stronge said.

In February 2024, a dispute arose when Baystreet purportedly terminated the contract with Midland when the works were “at or near practical completion”, and consequently allegedly did not pay Midland for certain works, Stronge contended.

Midland claimed the purported termination was invalid and a breach of contract. It said it was entitled to “substantial sums under the contract and in damages”.

Midland, with offices in Kells, Co Meath, referred the dispute to arbitration under a clause in the contract between the firms. Baystreet, with offices in Ballsbridge, Dublin, ceased its participation in the arbitration process in September 2025, and subsequently entered voluntary liquidation.

In a decision in February, arbitrator David O’Leary found the contract termination was unlawful, and awarded Midland €9,153,935.32, including interest and damages.

Stronge said it was necessary to make the application before the court as Baystreet had not made any payment on foot of the award. He said Midland had been exposed to claims by its own subcontractors and suppliers on foot of the wrongful contract termination and related conduct.

Following an application moved by Paul O’Grady, barrister for Midland instructed by solicitor Cian Duffy, Barniville this week granted judgment in the amount of €9,861,567 against Baystreet. The judgment amount reflected continuing interest on the arbitrator’s award.

The judge also granted permission for the enforcement of the arbitrator’s award.

Arthur Cunningham, barrister for the liquidators of Baystreet, did not object to the application. Counsel said the liquidator was agreeable to admitting Midland as a creditor of Baystreet in the amount of €9.1 million, the value of the award at the time of the arbitration decision.

]]><![CDATA[Denis O’Brien’s five-star Camiral resort in Spain returns to profit]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/denis-obriens-camiral-resort-returns-to-profit/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/denis-obriens-camiral-resort-returns-to-profit/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:21:30 +0000The group owned by businessman Denis O’Brien that operates the five-star Camiral resort in Girona in Spain last year returned to profit, with pretax profits of £826,000 (€988,000). The resort will host golf’s Ryder Cup in 2031.

It will be the second time Spain has hosted the Ryder Cup, 34 years after Seve Ballesteros captained Europe to victory at Valderrama in 1997.

Consolidated accounts filed to the UK’s Companies House show that Murryhill Holdings Ltd returned to profit as revenues surged by 49 per cent from £38.8 million to £57.86 million (€69.2 million) in 2025.

The principal activity of the group is the construction, promotion, marketing and operation of the Camiral resort.

In a note with the accounts the directors said that this activity includes the construction and sale of residential homes and apartments, the operation of a leisure complex including golf courses, a hotel and wellness facility.

The group’s revenues are made up of construction and hotel revenues; construction revenues increased by 123 per cent from £13.9 million to £31.08 million.

The group’s revenues also include a “service revenue” which rose by 7 per cent from £24.9 million to €26.7 million.

Camiral has two golf courses on the resort’s 540-hectare forested estate and has been a regular host of big international events, including three editions of the Open de España and the DP World Tour’s Catalunya Championship.

The resort also includes a five-star Camiral hotel and the 50-bedroom purpose-built boutique Lavida hotel.

The pretax profit of £826,000 follows a pretax loss of £2.56 million in 2024 – a positive swing of £3.38 million.

The pretax profit also takes account of non-cash depreciation, amortisation and impairment costs of £3.07 million.

The profit also takes into account interest payable of £1.22 million offset by a share of profits in associates received of £1.26 million.

Operating lease costs last year totalled £1.63 million.

The business continued to expand in 2025 with it paying out £5.74 million to acquire tangible fixed assets; this followed a payout of £5.18 million under that heading in 2024.

Staff numbers increased from 389 to 414.

Staff costs rose from £10.64 million to £11.86 million.

The ultimate parent entity of Murryhill Holdings Ltd is the Isle of Man-registered Distell Ltd and the accounts state that “the ultimate beneficial owner of the Group is Denis O’Brien”.

]]>HAROLD ABELLAN<![CDATA[Former HealthBeacon Ireland head fined €67,580 for insider trading ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/former-healthbeacon-employee-fined-67580-for-insider-trading/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/former-healthbeacon-employee-fined-67580-for-insider-trading/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 17:31:18 +0000A former executive with HealthBeacon, the medical devices company that slid into examinership in 2023, has been fined €67,580 by the Central Bank of Ireland for insider trading as he sold shares in the company.

The regulator said that Alan Dalton, who was HealthBeacon’s contracts manager and head of Ireland between 2018 and 2022, sold shares in the company on two separate occasions within weeks of leaving the company while in possession of price-sensitive company information, before it published a trading update that caused its shares to fall sharply.

Dalton avoided a loss of €21,800 by selling his shares when he did, the Central Bank added in a statement. Shares in the company slumped as much as 45 per cent on the day of the announcement.

Neither the company nor any of its other employees or agents were the subject of this investigation, it said.

Dalton resigned and ceased working for the company on June 24th, 2022. The trades took place in the weeks following his resignation.

“Trading while in possession of inside information, especially when an individual is in a privileged position to hold such information, is an abuse of the system and undermines the integrity of the market and as such is viewed very seriously by the Central Bank,” said Karen O’Leary, director of enforcement with the Central Bank.

“This outcome demonstrates the Central Bank’s willingness to investigate suspicious transaction and order reports (STORs) received from market intermediaries and follow our investigations through to the appropriate conclusion, holding those engaging in market abuse to account.”

Dalton could not immediately be reached at a company listed on his LinkedIn profile as his current employer.

HealthBeacon floated on the Irish stock market in December 2021 with an ambition of accelerating the roll-out of its flagship product, a digital sharps disposal bin for needles and syringes that reminds patients to maintain injection schedules at home. However, it filed for court protection from its creditors through an examinership application in late 2023 as it ran out of cash following a series of missed financial targets, including device sales, revenues and earnings.

The company was acquired from examinership in early 2024 for €6.9 million by Hamilton Beach Brands, a US home appliances group that sells everything from coffee makers to air fryers.

This is the second time the Central Bank has imposed a penalty on an individual for insider trading, in breach of market abuse rules.

A panel of assessors set up by the Central Bank recommended in 2022 that high-profile businessman Philip Lynch be fined €75,000 and disqualified from being involved in a regulated financial services company for five years after it found he used inside information to buy shares in cider and beer maker C&C Group. The sanction was subsequently confirmed by the High Court.

Separately, the first insider-trading criminal conviction in the history of the State was secured in March 2024 when Declan Service, from Portrush, Co Antrim, pleaded guilty to using price-sensitive market information to sell shares in a pharmaceutical company, Open Orphan, in 2020.

In another case, An Garda Síochána arrested and questioned two men in November 2024 as part of an ongoing investigation into suspected insider trading.

The individual at the centre of that investigation, who cannot be named for legal reasons, is a veteran of the State’s international funds sector, sources said at the time. The other is said to be a broker who worked for the suspect.

The Irish Times subsequently established late last year that the investigation is focused on suspicious dealing in Applegreen shares carried out before the announcement in late 2020 that the company had received a takeover approach.

The two men who were arrested were in no way connected to Applegreen, one of the largest fuel and forecourt retailers in the Republic.

Meanwhile, gardaí arrested and questioned four men in the east of the State in late September as part of another investigation into suspected insider trading offences. They were subsequently released without charge and files are being prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP)

]]><![CDATA[High Court to hear bid to set aside arbitrator’s award against group that worked fund social homes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/12/high-court-to-hear-bid-to-set-aside-arbitrators-award-in-new-beginning-dispute/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/12/high-court-to-hear-bid-to-set-aside-arbitrators-award-in-new-beginning-dispute/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 18:05:15 +0000The High Court is to hear an application to set aside an arbitrator’s award against a debt advisory group that worked to provide social and affordable housing with funding from international capital.

New Beginning Management Services Ltd (NBMS) and New Beginning Development Services Ltd (NBDS) have been involved in providing, through partnership with global investors, funding for social and affordable homes leased to local authorities and approved housing bodies.

The New Beginning firms provided advisory and asset management services relating to social housing stock owned by a fund headed by a collective asset management vehicle called the Platform ICAV.

The Platform ICAV acts as an umbrella fund for the Irish Social Housing (ISH) Fund I, as well as several other funds.

Investment advice for the Platform ICAV came from London-based RoundShield Partners, which was subsequently replaced by RS ISH Advisors Ltd (RS ISH).

In 2024, the New Beginning firms brought High Court proceedings against the Platform ICAV and all those associated companies and funds seeking to restrain the termination of an agreement between them.

It was claimed a decision had been made that RoundShield investors would exit the ISH fund and that RoundShield had conspired to bring about the termination of that agreement.

New Beginning claimed it would result in more than halving the commercial return due to NBMS “and of destroying NBMS as a going concern with the loss of jobs”.

The respondents strongly denied the claims.

The matter went to arbitration, which Platform ICAV says resulted in a “decisive victory” for it.

New Beginning then applied to the High Court to have the arbitration award set aside.

The arbitration process took 22 months to complete.

In the meantime, Ross Maguire, chief executive of New Beginning, who is also a senior counsel and had sworn the affidavit for his company in the 2024 action, had brought his own personal claim against Platform ICAV, claiming the new proceedings were essentially the same issues as those in the arbitration.

Jack Logan, solicitor with Arthur Cox for the respondents, said in an affidavit in relation to the New Beginning application to set aside the arbitration decision, that last April a stay was placed by the High Court on Maguire’s personal proceedings pending the determination of the arbitration.

Notices for termination of the agreement with New Beginning took effect on September 23rd last.

Logan said the substance of the New Beginning firms’ set-aside application arose from an assertion that during the conduct of the arbitration they were “denied ... their choice of advocate” by virtue of a decision of the arbitrator handed down in March 2026.

Consequently, adequate attention could not be and was not given to issues in the arbitration, it was claimed.

Logan said he considered that all of those issues were addressed comprehensively in the arbitration and in the arbitrator’s partial final award.

The application to set aside was an attempt to avoid the effects of the outcome of the arbitration, Logan said.

It was also being done to “delay the inevitable”, which is the lawful termination of the agreement with New Beginning as well as the determination of the respondents’ application for the costs of the arbitration, he said.

In an application this week to High Court president Judge David Barniville, Michael McDowell, counsel for New Beginning, said he was looking for an early hearing of the set aside application.

The judge said that because he would be “uncomfortable” dealing with this, as he knew some of the parties personally, he had spoken to Judge Oisín Quinn, who will be able to hear the matter next month.

He adjourned the case and gave directions in relation to legal submissions in advance of the hearing.

]]>Chris Maddaloni<![CDATA[Irish reunification will be costly - here are the key decisions which will decide the size of the bill]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/the-key-political-choices-that-will-determine-the-cost-of-irish-reunification/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/the-key-political-choices-that-will-determine-the-cost-of-irish-reunification/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:41:03 +0000The economics of a united Ireland has been a disputed territory for years, with analysis ranging from claims of large gains to significant costs. How do we make sense of this?

A new analysis from Prof Stephen Kinsella of the University of Limerick – The Economics of Reunification – published by Fine Gael as part of its ardfheis initiative on the topic, provides a vital guide through the arguments.

It shows, above all, two things. One is that the costs depend crucially on what model is chosen, how it is implemented and crucial negotiations with the UK on the issue of pensions and debt. And second, that the long-term growth performance of Northern Ireland will be crucial in determining the economics of reunification and whether it can be financed.

There is no one answer to the question of what a united Ireland would cost. It all depends. And this underlines the vital role of planning and preparation.

Kinsella, who is an adviser to Tánaiste Simon Harris, draws on a range of previous work, much of it undertaken post-Brexit. He estimates that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about €3 billion to €25 billion.

This is obviously a huge range. But this is where the story lies. As the assumptions and political choices change, so do the potential costs.

Kinsella frames the issue of the economics of the reunification debate around two questions. The first is who should pay which parts of the difference between Northern Ireland’s income and its expenditure. The second is what structures can be put in place to improve convergence between income and productivity levels in Northern Ireland and the Republic.

Disposable income per household is 13 per cent higher south of the Border, and the FDI model has boosted the Republic’s economy and its public finances. In contrast, the North has a net fiscal deficit of €17 billion, funded by the UK exchequer. This does not transfer automatically to the costs of reunification, but it is important nonetheless.

In a best-case scenario, if the UK agreed to take on the historic cost of the North’s pensions bill and the debt interest on the part of the UK’s national debt which would be attributed to Northern Ireland, then much of the €17 billion deficit would fall away.

Kinsella assumes some additional costs would accrue to the Republic from investment and running a separate administration if a federal model was chosen. This is one of a range of integration models in the paper, which also includes what he calls a “managed integration” plan – involving phased harmonisation in areas such as pay and welfare rates over 15 years – and a costly scenario that harmonises everything at once.

This variety of political decisions on what form unification would take and who picks up various bills leaves a potential matrix of costs not only, of course, in year one but for many years into the future. Bringing public pay and welfare rates in the North up to the Republic’s level, for example, would be a hugely expensive exercise.

The most important decisions are:

The pensions and debt issue

What happens to the accrued pension liabilities of Northern Ireland public servants and those who qualify for a state pension has been a key difference over the years between those taking an optimistic and pessimistic view of the economic benefits of reunification. Added to this is the interest on the part of the UK national debt, allocated to Northern Ireland in relation to its size within the UK.

Together these sum to close to €10 billion of the €17 billion annual UK estimate of the Northern Ireland deficit.

Pay convergence

Partly relying on what model of unification is chosen, it is clear that, as Kinsella puts it, “a nurse, teacher or civil servant in Belfast would expect the same pay as one in Dublin and a pensioner or jobseeker in Derry would expect the same weekly payment as one in Cork.” This would cost between €2.3 billion and €12.4 billion on day one, depending on how the gaps are measured, according to the report.

Northern envy at Republic pay rates

Huge decisions would lie ahead in this area and on the wider issue of how – or whether – public services would be integrated. Savings might be expected here from unified structures, but this would mean job losses, and Kinsella warns that the gains might be modest enough.

The model chosen

Choosing between the different possible models for reunification also has an impact on the economics.

A key message is that trying to unite the two economies in an unplanned rush is potentially very expensive and would require strong growth in Northern Ireland to make the finances add up in any fashion.

So-called managed integration over 15 years would still carry a high cost, on his calculations. Extra investment needed to increase productivity in the North would also need to be factored in.

As Kinsella says in his conclusions, a key message is that political choices will drive the cost of reunification – “the price depends far more on decisions made by policymakers than on any fixed bill”. The pensions and debt issues are vital in the short term, while over time closing the pay and welfare gap is crucial.

In any scenario, the financing is complicated, requiring significant borrowing even if there is financial assistance from the UK or even the European Union (where other member states might look askance at the idea given the public-finance constraints they face).

For the financing to work, growth becomes vital. Northern Ireland has averaged 1.3 per cent a year GDP growth since the early 2000s. Under a managed transition scenario, this would need to rise – depending on the assumptions – to between 3 per cent and 4.7 per cent on average each year to underpin a funding model.

Kinsella concludes that “this is a high bar, but it is possible”. Other assumptions might lower the growth targets a bit – again showing the importance of the key decisions.

A key conclusion from reading the report is that the potential financial implications for the Republic and its citizens are significant. Kinsella points to a range of potential costs per head in the Republic, which runs from €650 in year one to more than €2,600, with ongoing significant costs in future years.

Cross-Border tax rules putting off employers and workers, says report

Ireland’s public finances give it leeway to fund reunification, but this still carries costs. “However the costs are shared,” Kinsella writes, “someone has to pay them year by year.”

Like previous work by economists John FitzGerald and Edgar Morgenroth, the report points to the investment needs of Northern Ireland in areas such as education and skills, infrastructure and other measures to boost productivity.

There are potential gains from unification, too, as – for example – corporate taxes are cut in the North, encouraging inward investment, and new trade opportunities open up as the Irish Border disappears and Northern Ireland becomes a full part of the EU.

The extent of the resulting dynamic is hugely difficult to model with any confidence, but the North’s lacklustre economic performance compared with the Republic does point to some potential gains.

As the report concludes, whether reunification happens is a political and constitutional question. But the economics will be vital, and the report again underlines the complexity of the task and the huge preparations which would be required.

]]>Bill_Vorasate<![CDATA[Panic over cyberattacks plays straight into the hands of those behind them]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/12/panic-over-cyberattacks-plays-into-hands-of-those-behind-them/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/12/panic-over-cyberattacks-plays-into-hands-of-those-behind-them/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Put the kettle on. Right now, everyone would benefit from sitting down and taking a few minutes to have a cup of something.

My weekend was largely spent calming people down after last week’s cyberattacks. Supermarket fridges got hacked, there were bomb threats to airlines and the week ended with several media organisations being evacuated due to more bomb threats.

Plenty of otherwise rational people took this as a reason for all-out panic and as a sign of the need to prepare for the end of time. Civilisation isn’t about to collapse and it’s time you had that cuppa.

All of the recent attacks or threats were designed to disrupt. That is in keeping with the experience of countries that previously held the presidency of the Council of the EU.

There was certainly some fiscal impact but the core goal was to cause disorder. Some stock was lost from fridges, some flights were rescheduled and David McCullagh regretted not grabbing his jumper.

Many people became preoccupied with thoughts of, “if the hackers could do this, then what else are they capable of?”.

That’s the wrong question to ask. They are capable of far worse, but you should be asking if doing so is really in their interest.

The big fear I kept hearing about was a national blackout. At their operational best, the most sophisticated hackers could knock out power in Ireland for about 12 hours. Weather is a far more powerful and probable threat to the grid than any malicious actor.

The goal of these disruptions, which are almost always caused by state-backed actors, is to cause fear. It may be Russia today, North Korea tomorrow or the Federated States of Micronesia at the weekend. Instilling fear and uncertainty is a key part of the package.

It probably doesn’t help that these attacks are usually backed up by disinformation campaigns. We need only look at how effective Russia’s disinformation campaign in Poland has been in damaging public support there for Ukraine to see how effective this can be.

The playbook is awfully similar to what we’re seeing here. Some legitimate concerns – which we have had in Ireland following these attacks – are exaggerated to exacerbate fear.

Having a range of goals also works in favour of cybercriminals. Some want to disrupt, some want to stoke fear, others want to steal information or money and quite a few have a cocktail involving elements of all of these. Variety of motive makes it tougher to defend as the method of attack will vary.

No matter what the goal is, it is most unlikely that an all-out attack on Ireland’s core systems is uppermost in the mind of any attackers. The truth is that it does not make sense on a cost-benefit analysis to engage in something at that level.

Attacking the fridges was a good test to see what could be done. Using anonymous accounts to spread bomb threats en masse was a low-to-no-cost means of causing disruption. Taking out the grid or worse? That involves a real commitment and potential blowback. Not from Ireland, oh no, but from those outside Ireland who would be irked.

Multinational data centres and other tech infrastructure here make for tasty targets. Attacking one or a few is certainly a reasonably likely scenario that state-backed cyber attackers will consider. Going for a true shutdown? That gets the Americans angry because it disrupts their businesses. The US government is more than capable of striking back in kind.

Ukraine blowing up three Yandex data centres caused chaos in Moscow. Cyber retaliation by the US government to a cyberattack on their tech giants would make that look like a nosebleed.

Even if the US threat wasn’t there, while Ireland may punch above its weight for its population and economy size, we are far from the juiciest target in the EU, let alone globally.

Besides, with far less risk and at far lower cost, those who caused chaos with our fridges, flights and media last week can get a great return on investment.

They have already got plenty of people afraid. People are fretting about what they might need to do for an improbable attack. Many are realising that they aren’t really capable personally of doing much about it if anything did happen.

Having a torch or a charged power bank is sensible at the best of times. As I said earlier, weather is a real threat to power in this State and winter is coming.

There comes a point where obsessing over being ready for a threat you cannot do much about becomes unhealthy. It doesn’t take long for many people to hit that point.

Between two decades of covering cybersecurity and a lifelong interest in dystopian fiction, I’ve done my share of thinking about worst-case scenarios. Dying carefree beats the hell out of living in fear.

Yes, Ireland had a few mad days of it. It’ll have a few more wild ones in the days and weeks to come but UCD got promoted to football’s top domestic tier and you’ve made yourself a cuppa. Enjoy the good things and relax.

A. Transferring the property in a part-gift, part-loan arrangement works legally, but it may not be the most tax efficient option, says Carl Donnelly, head of tax at accountancy firm Cronin.

“You may end up paying more in total tax than if you made an outright gift,” says Donnelly.

In transferring the property to his son, the father will be liable for capital gains tax (CGT) as though he were selling it at its full market value of €490,000. This is regardless of whether the transfer is, in part, structured as a loan, says Donnelly.

The father is right. The law will let him use the CGT he owes as a credit against any capital acquisitions tax (CAT) arising for the son. This is because both taxes arise on the same event and the same property, says Donnelly.

A part-gift still qualifies for this offset. However, Revenue practice is to only give credit for the share of the CGT that relates to the gift element – €200,000 in this case.

“That amounts to 200/490ths of the CGT he owes on the property,” says Donnelly.

]]>Sinenkiy<![CDATA[Is the European Union getting real about ending tech dependence?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/11/is-the-european-union-getting-real-about-ending-tech-dependence/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/11/is-the-european-union-getting-real-about-ending-tech-dependence/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000

Europeans are afraid – very afraid – of their dependence on foreign digital technology.

A recent poll by the Bertelsmann Foundation finds almost three-quarters of European Union (EU) citizens worry that critical digital services “could be remotely disabled by actors outside Europe”. The same overwhelming majority think it important Europe should have “control over key digital technologies”.

As in other cases (such as Europeans’ negative reactions to the EU trade “deal” with Donald Trump last year), the bloc’s citizens are clear about what they want – and it’s not what they are getting at the moment. So how are European governments, and the EU in particular, going about delivering the “control” that voters demand?

Europe depends on other economies for much of the digital technology “stack”: the US for software, Taiwan for microchips, China for swathes of hardware. A first question, then, is how much of the stack needs to be home-grown inside the EU.

When I ask this of Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission vice-president in charge of tech sovereignty, she lists AI (artificial intelligence) models, semiconductors, quantum technology, satellites and the cloud as areas where Europe needs its own productive capacity. She does not go as far as self-sufficiency; the objective is “that we shouldn’t have risky dependencies [or be] dependent on one company or one third country”.

That is an ambitious list of sectors nonetheless, given how far behind Europe is. It is certainly sufficiently demanding that we must ask whether pursuing it would come at the cost of falling further behind and of giving up foreign frontier technology for the sake of inferior home-made versions. What does Brussels think about that trade-off?

US voters have rejected data centres and AI. What happens now?

It may not be that dramatic, Virkkunen suggests. “Sometimes we know that some companies ... want to give the impression that they always have the best services and the competitors don’t ... and it’s not always true,” she tells me.

She argues that the home-grown alternatives are sometimes just smaller and lesser known, rather than uncompetitive on quality or price. But that means the public sector can catalyse domestic substitutes by playing its role as a customer right.

Is the European public sector doing that, though? Many smaller EU-based digital companies feel they have a good product but government customers prefer to stick with the big providers they are used to. The commissioner accepts there is a degree of inertia. There is also a need to be “creative”, she says, to facilitate smaller companies coming together in consortiums to provide the scale of supply needed.

The biggest challenge, though, is access to funding for EU tech companies – not because of a lack of savings but thanks to Europe’s failure to channel financing to risky ventures. EU institutions as well as member states are starting to remedy this: a new scale-up fund is now operational and Brussels aims for more public-sector strategic “anchor” equity to crowd in private investors.

But so far the amounts being mobilised seem far too small compared to the hundreds of billions put into US tech investments every year. And by all accounts, talks over the EU’s next multiyear budget are whittling down further the amounts Brussels had originally proposed for new priorities including digital industrial policy.

On legislative reforms, too, from “EU Inc” (a pan-EU corporate entity) to localisation rules for sensitive digital services, member states are delaying or watering down proposals where Brussels already seemed to have been cautious not to ask for too much.

Virkkunen naturally avoids criticising national capitals. But she agrees that in the budget talks, “it’s very important that the member states keep the ambition there” for funding new technologies and defence. And not just to build domestic capacity, but because “the idea is that they should be able to compete globally”.

Ultimately, Brussels, while ambitious, seems to be aiming somewhere in between how far voters want to go and how far national governments are ready to move.

That means there are political rewards to be had for leaders bold enough to go further and faster. In the Bertelsmann poll, less than half of those asked think foreign providers are successfully held to European rules and expectations. It’s now up to politicians to convince them otherwise. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

Although full top-up payments are common in the public sector, meaning employees receive their full salary during maternity leave, employers are not legally obligated to provide maternity pay for their employees, Grassick says.

This means the “norm” may vary significantly in the private sector, depending on the industry you work in and the size of the business, she says.

“If a business has opted to provide a top-up payment for the duration of your maternity leave, or even for a period of that time, this would be considered an additional benefit rather than a statutory requirement,” she says.

An examination of the details of the transaction, which were lodged recently at the Land Registry, shows that a company called Raze Unlimited secured ownership of the property on July 17th. An inspection of the company’s filings with the Isle of Man Companies Registry shows that the firm was incorporated on June 4th last with McKillen’s close associate, Liam Cunningham, taking up the role of director alongside former AIB director and well-known financial adviser Bernard Somers. While the €12 million McKillen paid for the former Ormond Hotel is a multiple of the price Monteco Holdings paid for the property in 2013, it is still far short of the €17 million developer Bernard McNamara splashed out on the hotel’s purchase a year after its closure, in 2006. McNamara put it back on the market in 2009 shortly after his various businesses began to experience financial difficulty, with an asking price of €7 million, but the hotel, which features in the Sirens chapter of Ulysses, failed to sell.

In 2017, and following a protracted planning process, Monteco secured planning permission for the development of a new 120-bedroom hotel on the site, along with food, beverage and meeting facilities distributed across 5,850sq m (62,970sq ft) over seven floors.

Contacted for comment on his plans for the site, McKillen said: “I’m delighted to be part of the consortium that has acquired the Ormond Hotel. I want to tap into the vast experience and expertise of my three sons and hope they will play an active part in giving this amazing project the attention and vision it deserves.”

]]><![CDATA[Dublin city centre evolving to meet strength of hotel demand from visitors and investors]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/11/11/dublin-city-centre-evolving-to-meet-strength-of-hotel-demand-from-visitors-and-investors/https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/11/11/dublin-city-centre-evolving-to-meet-strength-of-hotel-demand-from-visitors-and-investors/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 05:35:00 +0000Few European cities kept their hotels as full as Dublin did this year. Occupancy reached nearly 85 per cent in the 12 months to September, according to CoStar, despite the headwinds facing global travel in 2026.

To understand the trend properly, I looked at visitor and occupancy data and spoke to a number of hoteliers. A decline in visitor numbers followed the outbreak of war in Iran and ran into early spring while the World Cup in the US had an impact on the tourist spend that would ordinarily have come to Ireland in early summer. However, the market recovered strongly through the rest of the busy season and beyond, and the data bears that out.

I attended the Irish Tourism Industry Confederation (ITIC) conference at Dublin’s Convention Centre in October to get a better sense of sentiment across the sector. The feedback from operators at the conference broadly reflected this view. The confederation highlighted a slight year-on-year decline in North American visitor numbers during August, which was attributed to fewer US travellers visiting for the College Football Classic than in previous years.

The issue of hotel room rates is more complex. According to CoStar, average room rates grew by 1.3 per cent in the nine months to September compared with 2025, with the average daily rate (ADR) reaching €177.80, a strong level for a market running at such high occupancy. This growth has not kept pace with Ireland’s consumer price index, however, which has run at more than 3 per cent over the same period.

Overall, the fact that occupancy held at such a high level this year despite such pressures is evidence of the market’s underlying resilience. Higher fuel costs and impending increases in the price of travel are the challenge for the winter months.

Irish weather

One of the most interesting contributions at the ITIC conference came from US ambassador to Ireland Ed Walsh, who spoke about the growing appreciation Americans have for the Irish summer, particularly the one just gone. Heatwaves have become more common across southern Europe in July and August in recent years, and northern European destinations have benefited as a result. Ireland’s famously unpredictable and changeable weather may well have become one of its greatest selling points.

The ambassador was also upbeat on the prospects for Irish-American tourism. He pointed to the potential for further events such as a college basketball game to extend the event calendar into the quieter winter months.

The Ryder Cup, the NFL and a strong events pipeline

Looking ahead, the events calendar is just as encouraging. The Ryder Cup at Adare Manor will be among the largest sporting events Ireland has ever hosted, with 280,000 spectators expected, and hotels are already booking out well beyond Limerick.

Beyond golf, last year’s inaugural NFL regular season game at Croke Park was among the best weekends Dublin hoteliers have experienced over the last decade, with room rates spiking sharply across the city. The NFL is expected to return, potentially within the next two years. U2 will play an Irish date next year as part of their global tour, Dublin will host several games at Euro 2028 and the proposed 20,000-capacity arena in the docklands, being developed by OVG and Live Nation, would add a year-round source of events.

Why Dublin hotels attract capital

Demand like this has not gone unnoticed. Sustained high occupancy over the last number of years has brought increased focus from developers and investors on a sector that historically has not been considered alongside core commercial or residential assets.

Last year the Irish market saw its largest-ever hotel transaction, with Pandox, one of Europe’s largest hotel property companies, acquiring Dalata Hotel Group for about €1.4 billion, the majority of which were Irish assets. Few deals do more to show how sought-after Dublin hotels have become.

Dublin hotels are utilitarian by nature. That is, they sit beside stadiums, convention centres, the airport or other transport hubs. When one considers the convenience of their location and the ongoing undersupply of rooms in the Dublin market, it’s easy to understand how such a high level of capital was deployed in a single deal.

€1bn pipeline

That faith on the part of investors is also showing up in new supply. Dublin’s hotel stock is on course to pass 30,000 rooms for the first time by 2028, with a substantial pipeline of new bedrooms due to deliver over the next two years. At an estimated development cost of €250,000 to €300,000 per key, the committed pipeline of more than 3,500 rooms represents a gross development value of between €0.9 billion and €1.1 billion, a significant statement of confidence in the long-term fundamentals of the market. The majority of this new supply consists of budget, long-stay and midscale accommodation.

Evolving city centre

The city centre is evolving in its composition, a trend I examined in an Irish Times article in July 2024, What impact will remote working have on the future of Dublin city centre? One of the central findings was that the city would move towards a greater mix of hotel, residential and living sector uses over time. And that has increasingly been borne out.

Some developers are now repurposing city-centre buildings for hotel use, and a number of former banks and retail units have planning permission for it. The former Cafe Kylemore on O’Connell Street was recently sold with permission for a boutique hotel, and a five-star hotel is planned for the former Ulster Bank premises at College Green, to name two. Not every project materialises, however. Numbers 5-9 Frederick Street South came to market with a feasibility study showing hotel potential, but was acquired, refurbished and upgraded as an office scheme, now let to Cantor Fitzgerald.

What comes next

Adding more than 3,500 rooms to a market this full should bring some normalisation of trading levels. The events pipeline, record passenger numbers through Dublin Airport, and Fáilte Ireland’s sharp focus on growing visitor numbers all point in the right direction. Dublin remains one of the more attractive European hotel markets for investors.

Colin Richardson is a senior director and head of research at CBRE Ireland

]]><![CDATA[How to save on car insurance: Actuaries reveal 10 insider secrets ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/11/how-to-save-on-car-insurance-actuaries-reveal-10-insider-secrets/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/11/how-to-save-on-car-insurance-actuaries-reveal-10-insider-secrets/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Are you paying too much for car insurance? The average premium is up a whopping 18 per cent since 2022, according to Central Bank figures.

There are few household bills where we would tolerate this jump. You can suck it up, or you can take action to lower your quote. And actuaries have the inside track.

The average car insurance premium last year was €655, an increase of €144 in just three years. But you don’t have to accept another expensive renewal.

Actuaries know exactly what insurers look for when calculating a premium. Understanding their secrets could help you get a cheaper quote. Here are 10 tips to save on your next policy.

1. Check your mileage

Which drivers present the highest risk? Those who spend the most time on the road. One of the best predictors of a car crash is how much time you spend driving, says actuary Noel Garvey, who is chairman of the Society of Actuaries’ general insurance committee.

That’s why insurers ask your estimated annual mileage when quoting for your policy.

“The more you drive, the higher the chance of an accident,” says Garvey. More mileage means more risk, so insurers will charge you more.

Close to one million people reported working from home at least sometimes in the second quarter of 2026, according to Central Statistics Office (CSO) figures. If you are one of them, tell your insurer.

The average private car in Ireland covered 15,196km in 2023, according to the CSO. Many people drive less.

To check your mileage, divide the odometer reading by the car’s age in years, says Motorcheck.ie. Or check the readings between NCT certificates, work out the difference in mileage and compare it to the national average.

Overestimating your mileage when seeking a quote means paying more than you need to. But you need to play fair. Underestimating to save money could cause problems if you need to claim.

Why is motor insurance so expensive in Ireland?

2. Excess

You don’t have to be an actuary to get a better price on car insurance but it pays to know more about how your quote is designed, says Garvey.

Ask your insurer how the price changes if you increase the excess, he says. This is the amount you agree to pay towards a claim. It’s often set at a default of €250 to €300.

If there’s a crash and you submit a claim for €4,000 and your policy excess is €200, for example, you’ll pay the first €200 and the insurance company will pay €3,800.

Agreeing to a higher excess could mean a cheaper quote.

“If you back yourself to be more careful than most, it might be well worth taking on that risk,” says Garvey.

Just ensure the excess you set is affordable in case of a mishap.

3. Drive the right car

Buying a new or second-hand car? Get an insurance quote before signing on the dotted line, says Garvey. Some cars will be more expensive to insure than others, tying you into higher premiums throughout your ownership.

Cars with smaller engines, lower repair costs and strong safety ratings can be cheaper to insure, says an Aviva spokesperson.

Of the most popular car models on Irish roads, the cheapest to insure, on average, are the Hyundai Tucson (€569), the Nissan Qashqai (€584) and the Skoda Octavia (€585), according to data from the chill.ie car insurance pricing index, published in July. The most expensive at €783 were the BMW Series.

Owners of big horsepower, seven-seater SUVs will pay a whole lot more.

Buyers of all-electric vehicles, now the best-sellers on the Irish market, will likely make significant savings on fuel, but you will need to factor higher insurance into your running costs.

“Electric vehicles can be more expensive to insure than a petrol or diesel car as they are, in general, more expensive to repair,” says Garvey.

On the flip side, electric cars are responsible for 5 to 10 per cent fewer crashes on average than comparable vehicles with internal combustion engines, according to a study by the German Insurance Association.

Damage caused by electric vehicles are up to 20 per cent less frequent than conventional vehicles, the study said. This could be due to drivers planning ahead or driving more slowly to preserve battery.

But the damage caused by electric cars, which are heavier, and the damage caused to them, tends to be more expensive to repair, the study said.

4. Get a black box

A telematics driving policy, also called “black box” insurance, can knock thousands off the insurance policy premium for first-time drivers or those new to Ireland.

The policy uses a device fitted to your car or a phone app to monitor things like your mileage, speed, acceleration and braking patterns, how you take corners, the amount of time you are driving by day and night and on urban and rural roads, says Garvey.

What are telematics policies, and how can they knock thousands off motor insurance costs?

Price comparison website bonkers.ie sought quotes from a range of providers, including AIG, Aviva and Zurich, under a number of conditions and found that a 20-year-old driver with a full licence could get a quote of just €570 for fully comprehensive telematics cover.

When there was no telematics cover, the price of the standard policy jumped to almost €3,900.

Depending on how safely they drive, they may benefit from more personalised pricing on renewal, says Aviva Ireland.

Before signing up, check for restrictions such as curbs on distance or night-time driving, Garvey advises.

“Lower mileage or safer driving does not guarantee a lower premium from every insurer and it’s important to compare a telematics quote against a standard quote of comparable cover before purchase,” he says.

5. Optional cover

Your car policy can come with a boot-load of extras. Breakdown assist, cover for lost or stolen keys, loss of personal belongings, windscreen cover, courtesy car replacement, cover for legal fees to recover uninsured losses – the list is long.

Some of these “extras” are bundled into the price; some will cost you more.

“Check what’s included as standard, what is the optional extra and whether you actually need it,” says Garvey.

Lost key cover pays to replace lost or stolen keys and can add about €20 to your quote. If your home insurance policy already covers this, or if you are comfortable paying for a rare key replacement, skip it and save yourself some dosh.

Likewise, if you already have breakdown assist through a manufacturer’s warranty, don’t pay on the double.

If you have built up several years of no claims, paying extra for no-claims discount protection can be worth considering. A single claim without protection could reset your discount to zero, significantly increasing your premium at renewal.

Stepback no-claims discount protection can be a more affordable alternative to full protection. Your discount reduces after a claim rather than disappearing entirely. Some insurers may offer this as standard.

How common are car fires?

6. Drop to one car

If your household has two cars and one spends most of its time sitting in the drive, dropping to one car will save you thousands.

Typically, in a two-car household both members have “main driver” status on their respective policies, with individual no-claims bonus records. You probably have “named driver” cover on each other’s policies too.

You might think you need to keep two cars with main driver insurance policies going to maintain your no-claims bonus; you may not, depending on your insurer. You can be a named driver only and keep your no-claims bonus, provided you swap main driver status with your partner or spouse every two years.

“Our no-claims discount remains valid for up to two years after a customer’s previous policy expires, subject to terms and conditions,” says an Aviva spokesperson.

When you finish your two-year stint as the main driver, be sure to ask your insurance provider for written proof of your no-claims record. Keep this on file.

Garvey advises customers to check directly with their insurer how long an unused no-claims bonus remains valid and whether time spent solely as a named driver affects its recognition.

If your household has two cars, be aware that a no-claims discount is earned separately on each vehicle, says Aviva.

“Each vehicle must have the appropriate insurance cover in place, so simply alternating who is the main policyholder every two years would not in itself provide cover for two cars.”

But if the household has one car, named driver experience is treated separately and may be recognised where someone has built up a claim-free driving record as a named driver.

Aviva policyholders may have third-party cover to drive other people’s cars, but this extension on a policy applies to the policyholder only, says Aviva. The named driver shouldn’t assume they have this extended cover.

EV public charging costs now exceeding those for petrol and diesel

7. Be like Louth

Penalty points are the surest way to drive up your insurance cost. Drive better and you’ll pay less.

The people of Louth got the memo. Just 10.9 per cent of its licensed motorists hold active penalty points – the lowest in the State, according to analysis of Road Safety Authority and Central Statistics Office data by Quote Devil this year.

Wexford is Ireland’s penalty points capital. More than one in five drivers there have active points on their licence, twice the rate of Louth.

Speeding and holding a mobile phone while driving are the most common offences, each carrying an immediate three penalty points, according to the data.

“Once you reach three or more penalty points, many insurers increase premiums or apply steep surcharges,” says Quote Devil.

Border counties lead the State in penalty points for uninsured driving, while Cork drivers have the most for failing to wear a seat belt. Leitrim, Kerry and Roscommon drivers are the most likely to have points for worn tyres.

“Having active penalty points or a motoring conviction can make finding affordable car insurance challenging. Many standard insurers penalise point-holders heavily,” says Quote Devil.

Insurance claims are another issue. They comprise injury to people and damage to vehicles, says Garvey. While injury costs in Ireland have gone down, more than half the money paid out on settled claims now goes towards damage repair costs.

A study by Swiss Re found that Waymo’s autonomous vehicles had an 88 per cent reduction in property damage claims and a 92 per cent reduction in bodily injury claims compared to human driver baselines. When it comes to insurance costs, the driver is a significant variable.

Polestar’s future-gazing new concept is far more rational than it appears

8. Pay annually

Paying for your car insurance in instalments can ease the blow to your monthly budget, but this can mean extra charges.

“The total paid over the year may be higher than the headline annual premium,” says Garvey. “Look at the overall cost, not just the monthly instalment when comparing quotes.”

Pay the yearly amount upfront if you can, even if that means dipping into your savings, or start to put a little bit of money away each month now so that you can pay in full next year, says Mabs.

9. Don’t modify

Thinking of buying a modified car or modifying your own? Engine modifications, changes to the wheels, suspension or bodywork can all drive up your quote.

“Modifications can affect an insurer’s assessment of the vehicle’s risk, value or likely repair cost, so you should disclose them and check the potential insurance impact before making changes,” says Garvey.

Boy racers take note.

10. Shop around

Automatically renew your policy with your existing insurer and you will pay more. Too many of us do this: maybe that’s why net profit among Irish motor insurers hit €89 million last year.

Put half an hour into shopping around and you could save around €100.

When you get your renewal policy documents and quote this year, ask for a discount, says Garvey.

You could use a comparison website like bonkers.ie, switcher.ie, chill.ie to compare quotes. You’ll need your penalty points status – you can request a statement on ndls.ie, using your PPS number.

You’ll need details of any claims in the past five years too. You’ll find those in your current policy documents.

If you are shopping around by phone, ask if it’s cheaper for you to complete the transaction online. Many insurers provide an online discount.

And if there is more than one car in your household, ask your insurer for a multipolicy discount.

   <title>Finanzchefin Kress soll Nvidia auf Kurs halten</title>
   <description>Der Rückzug von Nvidia-Gründer Jensen Huang nach seinen Affären bringt Finanzchefin Colette Kress beim Chipriesen nach 13 Jahren ins Rampenlicht. Mit dem rasanten Aufstieg der Firma zum Motor des KI-Booms spielte sie angesichts der explosiven Umsatzentwicklung bereits eine Schlüsselrolle. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447982/">
   <title>Putin bleibt bei Forderungen</title>
   <description>Russlands Präsident Wladimir Putin hat eine Abkehr von Moskaus Forderungen für ein mögliches Ende des russischen Angriffskrieges in der Ukraine ausgeschlossen. Bei einem Treffen mit den US-Vermittlern Steve Witkoff und Jared Kushner am Donnerstag im Kreml wies Putin eine mögliche Einigung zurück, die entmilitarisierte Zonen zwischen den Stellungen vorsehen würde. Witkoff und Kushner reisten noch am Abend nach Dublin und verkündeten dort gemeinsam mit dem ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj, dass Europa bei den nächsten Friedensgesprächen dabei sein würde.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447983/">
   <title>WKStA prüft Verfahren gegen Orden</title>
   <description>An vier ihrer sieben Spitalsstandorte in Österreich betreiben die Barmherzigen Brüder Apotheken mit einer Doppelfunktion: Sie versorgen die ordenseigenen Spitäler, beliefern gleichzeitig aber auch andere Kliniken und sind für die Öffentlichkeit zugänglich. Derzeit stehen Vorwürfe im Raum, der Orden habe seinen eigenen Krankenhäusern Medikamente mit enormen Aufschlägen verkauft und sich dadurch Steuergelder in Millionenhöhe erschlichen. Wie ORF.at gegenüber am Donnerstag bestätigt wurde, wird der Fall inzwischen von der Wirtschafts- und Korruptionsstaatsanwaltschaft (WKStA) geprüft. Eine Entscheidung über etwaige Ermittlungen soll in ein „paar Tagen“ fallen.</description>

After Russia announced that it had dismantled a Polish spy network and arrested two alleged agents, Poland has dismissed the claims as “disinformation” and a “provocation”.

On Wednesday, while Poland was celebrating its national Independence Day, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had “disrupted the activities of an intelligence network of the Polish special services operating in Kaliningrad”, a Russian exclave that borders Poland.

It claimed to have detained two “agents”- one working for Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW), the other for the Internal Security Agency (ABW) – who had been “collecting and transmitting information about military personnel and facilities” and “the socio-economic situation in the Kaliningrad region”.

 

The FSB added that seven Polish citizens and three Russians who had had contact with Polish intelligence agencies had been “officially warned”, and that the Polish citizens had been banned from entering Russia.

The agency also published a film containing images of alleged suspects being detained and various documents and telephone messages in Polish.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the arrests would not further worsen relations with Poland given ties between the two countries “essentially do not exist right now,” reported the RIA news agency.

 

In a statement on Wednesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for Poland’s security services, said that he regarded the Russian announcement “as yet another provocation and act of disinformation”, especially as it had been released on Polish Independence Day.

He added that he would not comment further and “appealed to everyone not to amplify hostile narratives or play into Russian propaganda”.

Speaking to news website Wirtualna Polska, Maciej Wewiór, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, said that Poland was working to verify the information announced by the FSB.

However, he urged “extreme caution” when dealing with such claims from Russia. “Let’s not fall for Russian propaganda and become pawns in this game,” he said.

Jako rzecznik ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych nie komentuję materiałów zamieszczanych w sieci przez rosyjskie służby.
🛑 W dniu Narodowego Święta Niepodległości traktuję je szczególnie jako kolejną prowokację i dezinformację.
🛑 Apeluję o niepowielanie wrogiej narracji i…

— Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) November 11, 2026

Polish fact-checking and investigative journalism service OKO.press also raised doubts about the material shared by Russia. It notes that the alleged Polish-language phone messages released by the FSB have unnatural wording and appear to have been translated from Russian.

It also points out that the footage showing the alleged detentions appears to have been recorded much earlier, judging by the green folliage on trees.

This assessment was echoed by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the security services from 2016 to 2022. He said that “fabricated propaganda materials” were clearly “prepared in advance” and “fit the Russian security services’ ongoing campaign against Poland”.

“It should be assumed that, in its operation against Poland, Moscow will resort to fabricated evidence, and today’s FSB statement will be used to legitimise earlier accusations against Poland of preparing an attack on Kaliningrad,” he added.

#InfoAlert. Kolejna rosyjska prowokacja. FSB twierdzi, że rozbiła polską siatkę szpiegowską pracującą w Obwodzie Królewieckim. Analiza komunikacji rosyjskiej wskazuje, że mamy do czynienia z zaplanowaną sekwencją działań informacyjnych. Wpisuje się ona w stałe oddziaływanie… pic.twitter.com/s6bTV9pIK8

— Stanisław Żaryn (@StZaryn) November 11, 2026

The FSB’s announcement came a week after Poland announced that it had detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components, which were smuggled over the border into Kaliningrad.

Poland also sent additional security personnel to its regions along the Russian border this month following intelligence reports suggesting a planned act of sabotage or other provocation there.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk later claimed that “individuals with flashlights” had been spotted at the border but “we very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and managed to prevent a provocation”.

Poland recently launched a special operation along the Russian border after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days.

For more, see our report from yesterday:https://t.co/RVaXb6SQJI

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2026

Poland has seen a sharp rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Moscow in recent years.

The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined.

Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe.

In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates on its territory, prompting Russia to do the same with Polish consulates in a tit-for-tat move.

Polish prosecutors have filed an indictment against a Ukrainian man accused of working on behalf of Russian intelligence and assisting in last year’s sabotage of a rail line in Poland.

The accused, who can be named only as Volodymyr B. under Polish privacy law and is pictured above, will stand trial for espionage, sabotage and causing the risk of a major transport accident. He could face up to life in prison if convicted.

Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK skierował do Sądu Okręgowego w Warszawie akt oskarżenia przeciwko Volodymyrowi B. w śledztwie dotyczącym aktów dywersji na torach kolejowych, do których doszło jesienią 2025 r. w miejscowości Mika i Gołąb. ⬇️https://t.co/N2vK7thpKe

— Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026

In November last year, the Polish authorities discovered acts of sabotage on two sections of a rail line running between Warsaw and the eastern Polish city of Lublin.

In one case, a device containing military-grade C4 explosive was detonated in an apparent attempt to derail a freight train near the village of Mika. However, it caused only minor damage to the floor of the train.

The following day, in the nearby town of Puławy, a passenger train carrying 475 people had to brake suddenly due to damage to the line. However, no one was injured.

A picture released by police showing damage to a track as a result of the sabotage

Soon after, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that the perpetrators had been identified as two Ukrainian citizens working on behalf of Russia. They had entered Poland from Belarus and then fled back across the border immediately after the incident.

In December, Interpol issued red notices for the men, identified as Yevhenii Ivanov and Oleksandr Kononov. However, the pair remain at large.

Meanwhile, a third Ukrainian man, Volodymyr B., was detained in Poland a few days after the sabotage and was charged with assisting in carrying out the attack.

 

In their statement regarding the indictment of Volodymyr B., published on Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office says that he assisted Yevhenii Ivanov in conducting reconnaissance of the area, selecting a place to plant the explosives and installing recording devices and metal elements on the rails.

“These actions created an imminent threat of a disaster, threatening the lives and health of many people and significant property damage,” wrote prosecutors. “Their goal was to seriously intimidate many people and influence public opinion.”

They also say that Volodymyr B. was “participating in the activities of Russian intelligence”. The most serious charge he faces is for acts of sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of ten years, ranging up to life.

Interpol has published red notices for two men that Poland says were responsible for carrying out the sabotage of a rail line last month on behalf of Russia

The pair immediately fled to Belarus after the incident and their current location is unknown https://t.co/RnahHDQkC8

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 18, 2025

Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. Such actions have often been carried out by Ukrainians and Belarusians.

Last month, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

This week, Poland announced that it had detained and charged two Ukrainians accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia.

]]> Polish deputy foreign minister charged over alleged misappropriation of millions of zloty https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/12/polish-deputy-foreign-minister-charged-over-alleged-misappropriation-of-millions-of-zloty/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:30:00 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106632

A Polish deputy foreign minister has been charged with misappropriating millions of zloty entrusted to him and taking steps to prevent creditors from recovering money owed to them.

Prosecutors say that Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski used the money for personal expenses and to buy three apartments in Warsaw. His wife has also been charged in the case. Both of them deny the allegations, and Bartoszewski says he “will defend the truth and my good name”.

Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK przedstawił posłowi na Sejm RP Władysławowi Teofilowi Bartoszewskiemu dwa zarzuty: przywłaszczenia powierzonych mu środków pieniężnych znacznej wartości oraz udaremnienia zaspokojenia wierzyciela.

Komunikat: ➡️ https://t.co/EXZ3NsovBh pic.twitter.com/Lmp2f3Bw2r

— Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026

The case dates back to before Bartoszewski had entered politics. In 2019, he became an MP for the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). In 2023, after PSL became a junior partner in the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, he was made deputy foreign minister.

From 2004, say prosecutors, Bartoszewski was entrusted with managing the assets of Polish art collector and philanthropist Andrzej Ciechanowiecki, who was Bartoszewski’s godfather and a friend of his late father, Władysław Bartoszewski, a former Polish resistance fighter, Auschwitz prisoner, and later foreign minister.

From 2005, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski, who has waived his right to anonymity in the case, also managed funds belonging to the Non Omnis Moriar Foundation, linked to the collector.

According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski used some of the money to buy and renovate three apartments in Warsaw between 2005 and 2006. From 2009, Ciechanowiecki began asking Bartoszewski to account for the funds, but he allegedly failed to do so and began avoiding contact with Ciechanowiecki.

 

In 2012, Ciechanowiecki and the foundation terminated their agreements with Bartoszewski and demanded the return of funds, say prosecutors. The following year, they filed a lawsuit demanding that Bartoszewski pay them around £1 million, 7.2 million zloty, €650,000 and $76,000, plus interest.

According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski then took steps to prevent the money from being recovered. A company owned by him and his wife sold three apartments in Warsaw, after which the couple disposed of their shares in the company. His wife also donated a property to their underage children.

“As a result of these actions, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and his wife possess no assets from which the creditor’s claims could be satisfied,” prosecutors said.

In March 2024, a Warsaw court ordered Bartoszewski to pay the foundation more than 13.2 million zloty, plus interest. Prosecutors note that the judgment is not yet binding as an appeal is still pending.

Od półtora roku sąd nie wyznaczył terminu apelacji w sprawie Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego — dowiedział się Onet. Sąd pierwszej instancji nakazał wiceministrowi spraw zagranicznych zwrot aż 13 mln zł, jakie powierzył mu jego chrzestny https://t.co/JzPwcJG4KU

— Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) November 4, 2025

Meanwhile, in 2023, representatives of the Ciechanowiecki Collection Foundation at the Royal Castle in Wawel, which now holds the assets of Ciechanowiecki (who died in 2015), filed a notification to prosecutors of alleged crimes committed by Bartoszewski and his wife.

Earlier this year, the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, asked parliament to lift Bartoszewski’s immunity so that prosecutors could bring charges against him. However, he voluntarily waived it on 6 October.

At the time, Bartoszewski told newspaper Fakt that he “absolutely does not feel guilty” and “the evidence confirms this”. He also claimed that there is “a political element to my case”, though he did not elaborate further.

Sejmowa komisja regulaminowa opowiedziała się we wtorek za uchyleniem immunitetu posła PSL Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego w związku z wnioskiem prokuratury w sprawie podejrzenia popełnienia przez niego między innymi przestępstwa przywłaszczenia mienia.https://t.co/ydA0jNNUQ8

— tvn24 (@tvn24) October 6, 2026

On Tuesday this week, prosecutors announced that they had charged Bartoszewski with misappropriation of funds of significant value – £1 million, €405,000 and 6,683,705 zloty – entrusted to him by Ciechanowiecki and the foundation. The offence carries a prison sentence of between one and 10 years.

A second charge concerns allegedly taking steps to prevent or reduce the recovery of money owed to a creditor. It carries a prison sentence of between three months and five years.

Prosecutors say that, on the same day, they “brought similar charges” against Bartoszewski’s wife and that both of the accused denied guilt.

Wiceszef MSZ Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski oświadczył, że nie przyznaje się do popełnienia zarzucanych mu przez prokuraturę czynów. Zapowiedział, że będzie bronił prawdy i swojego dobrego imienia "tak długo, jak będzie to konieczne". https://t.co/tGodfs9Gzi

— Interia (@Int_Wydarzenia) November 10, 2026

In a statement issued later on Tuesday, Bartoszewski issued a statement rejecting the allegations and saying that he “will defend the truth and my good name in every instance, for as long as necessary”, reports the Polish Press AGency (PAP).

“I am convinced that both the criminal proceedings and the ongoing civil proceedings will confirm my arguments and rights to my property,” he added.

“I consistently maintain that all actions related to the acquisition of the real estate were consistent with the original will of Andrzej Ciechanowiecki expressed at the time of their purchase, and the premises were intended to constitute permanent financial security for my family.”

Asked whether the prime minister would dismiss Bartoszewski following the charges or wait for a court ruling, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said that the deputy minister “is currently on leave and decisions regarding this matter will be made upon his return”.

]]> Annual Polish Independence March passes through Warsaw https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/11/annual-polish-independence-march-passes-through-warsaw/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:34:34 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106667
