The annual march held in Warsaw to mark Poland’s Independence Day has passed through the city without major incident. This year’s event took place amid heightened security following the deadly terrorist attack in Kraków just four days earlier.

Hundreds of thousands of people, including President Karol Nawrocki, marched through the city amid a sea of white-and-red flags. The event, which is organised by nationalist groups, also acted as a display of unity among the right-wing and far-right opposition ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections.

Figures from the more liberal government, as always, avoided the march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk celebrated Independence Day hundreds of kilometres away in the city of Szczecin, where he issued an invitation to the opposition-aligned Nawrocki to visit his home for talks.

Zapełnia się rondo im. Romana Dmowskiego. Cała transmisja z #marszuniepodległości w @TV_Trwam pic.twitter.com/TvMHypx8gn

— Michał Rybka (@_MRybka) November 11, 2026

This year’s Independence March was held under the slogan “Polak w Polsce gospodarzem”, which translates roughly as “Poles are in charge in their own country”.

The slogan was chosen to “emphasise our opposition to foreign influences on Poland and underscore that Poland should be a nation-state without mass immigration”, said Rafał Buca, the march’s spokesman. “In Poland, Poles should rule – not some foreigners, not the European Union, not big corporations.”

On the morning of the march, the organisers shared an image showing Tusk as a puppet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. “Time to cut the strings of foreign influence,” they declared.

Czas odciąć sznurki obcych wpływów i marionetkowych decyzji!

W naszym własnym kraju to my – polscy obywatele – jesteśmy jedynym suwerenem i to my ustalamy reguły!

🇵🇱 POLAK W POLSCE GOSPODARZEM! pic.twitter.com/8Htr8s0klx

— Marsz Niepodległości (@StowMarszN) November 11, 2026

The main organisers of the march are associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group that sits among the opposition in parliament. But it is attended by a wide range of people, from the mainstream right through to the radical right.

Leading figures from other opposition parties, including the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), were present, as well as Nawrocki, who last year became the first Polish president to attend the march.

A member of the march’s organising committee, Marcin Osowski, told broadcaster WNET that around half a million people were at today’s event. The municipal authorities, which are under the control of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, later put the figure at around 250,000.

That would make today’s Independence March the largest ever other than the one in 2018, when a broader event was organised to mark the centenary of Poland regaining its independence after World War One.

 

The opposition was aiming to show a united front amid their ongoing protests against the recent takeover of the constitutional court by a group of government-backed judges and ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections, at which they hope to unseat Tusk’s government.

“It’s about showing our strength and, at the same time, for this march to be a springboard for the election campaign,” said Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of PIS, during the march, quoted by the Niezależna news website. “Unity is important.”

Meanwhile, one of the leaders of Confederation, Krzysztof Bosak, told the crowd in a speech that, “while we have different experiences and views, under the white-and-red flag we form one community”.

“Next year, we must turn this community into an election victory…We must remove the current clique from power and form a pro-Polish government,” he declared. “We do not accept the violent takeover of state institutions. We demand respect for the law.”

Na Marszu Niepodległości jesteśmy u siebie! Przyjeżdżamy z różnych stron, mamy różne doświadczenia i poglądy, ale pod biało-czerwoną flagą tworzymy jedną wspólnotę. Każdy jest w niej potrzebny. Także ten, kto dziś czuje się samotny, odrzucony i traci poczucie sensu.

Ta wspólnota… pic.twitter.com/L5pYU1RVv0

— Krzysztof Bosak 🇵🇱 (@krzysztofbosak) November 11, 2026

However, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a picture of himself at the march in front of a banner showing images of both Tusk and Kaczyński crossed out, alongside the word “Reset”.

While Bosak’s nationalist faction of Confederation is seen as more amenable to the idea of working with PiS to form a potential future coalition government, Mentzen’s libertarian faction is less enthusiastic about the idea.

Nadchodzi, nadchodzi Marsz Niepodległości! 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/o8Tkf8673G

— Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) November 11, 2026

In the past, the march has sometimes seen violence, with participants clashing with police. However, in recent years it has generally passed peacefully, and that was again the case today.

The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaszkowski, who is a deputy leader of KO, said on Wednesday afternoon that, other than the illegal use of pyrotechnics (such as a flare held up by Mentzen), the march was proceeding without incident.

Local authorities in Warsaw had put in place additional security measures following Saturday’s terrorist attack in Kraków, in which a 24-year-old Polish man, Michał Oksiński, killed six people and injured over a dozen more by shooting an AR-15 rifle from his car.

Oksiński’s rampage was quickly brought to a halt in a shootout with armed police, and he died from his injuries on Monday. On Tuesday, the justice minister revealed that evidence uncovered so far shows “strong traces of right-wing extremism” in Oksiński’s activity.

There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister.

His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026

Tusk, meanwhile, celebrated Independence Day in the city of Szczecin in northwest Poland.

“All of us, without exception, are responsible for ensuring that Poland remains strong, secure, free and independent forever,” said the prime minister. “Everyone who holds Poland in their hearts must understand that independence, freedom and a secure republic are a common good.”

Tusk noted that, since the recent crisis around the constitutional court broke out, Nawrocki has refused his offer to meet and discuss how to find a solution to a crisis that has pitted judges appointed under the former PiS government against those chosen by the current ruling coalition.

The prime minister today renewed that offer, inviting Nawrocki and his family to visit Tusk’s home in the build-up to Christmas. “We must be able to discuss things together, without bitterness, without hatred,” said the prime minister.

Note: This article has been updated to include the official estimate of attendance at the march.

Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have signed a statement of intent on strengthening cooperation between their defence industries.

“Today, we are taking the next steps in our alliance,” declared Hegseth, while Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the move signalled that Poland is now “not only a model ally…but has become a strategic partner of the United States”.

The Polish defence minister added that he would also push for equipment jointly manufactured by Poland and the US to be eligible for EU defence funding. “Poland is the US ambassador in the EU,” he declared.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.

In its efforts to restore democracy, the government may sometimes take actions that are “not fully compliant with the law”, admits @donaldtusk.

But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

 

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia.

The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November.

The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​

🇫🇷🇬🇧 KOALICJA: The MNF-U is training to ensure a solid and lasting peace in Ukraine

The Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U), formed from the Coalition of the Willing and under 🇫🇷🇬🇧command, is launching its first major exercise: KOALICJA

📅 November 9–22, 2026
📍In Poland,… pic.twitter.com/Ikcl1uY8N2

— The 🇫🇷 Joint Staff – Military operations (@FrenchForces) November 7, 2026

The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition.

“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U.

The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”.

France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”.

 

Around 2,800 troops are being deployed for the manoeuvres, with AFP reporting that this includes 1,100 from France alone. The British defence ministry says it has sent 300 personnel, as well as Typhoon and Voyager aircraft.

In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey.

Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”.

However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support.

Nederland doet met enkele honderden militairen mee aan oefening Koalicja in Polen. De Coalition of the Willing traint er met 11 landen op snelle verplaatsing, commandovoering en bevoorrading ter voorbereiding op mogelijke steun aan Oekraïne na beëindiging van de oorlog. pic.twitter.com/JLE6W91HnZ

France says that the deployment of forces to Ukraine would include sending instructors to help the country rebuild and strengthen its armed forces, while air missions would enable civlian aircraft to resume flying in Ukrainian airspace.

At sea, MNF-U forces could help clear mines from shipping routes in the Black Sea. The maritime component of the current exercises is being led by Turkey through a simulated operational exercise, without deploying troops to Poland itself.

France, the UK and Poland have emphasised, however, that the MNF-U forces would only be deployed once fighting in Ukraine has ceased and would not carry out peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring duties.

On Saturday, the spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, Maria Zakharova, condemned the exercises, saying that they make “absolutely clear that the West remains unwilling to take Russia’s legitimate security concerns into account and continues to fuel the spiral of escalation”.

She described the deployment of any foreign armed forces to Ukraine as “absolutely unacceptable” and said they would “create additional threats to Russia’s security”.

“Any military units in Ukraine will be regarded by the Russian armed forces as legitimate targets, with all the risks and consequences that entails,” warned Zakharova.

Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova’s answer to a media question in connection with the first military exercises of the so-called Multinational Force – Ukraine under the Coalition of the Willinghttps://t.co/GiouEAmT6J

The exercises come as Ukraine and Russia meet the United States and others for peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week. Ukraine has repeatedly insisted that European security guarantees would be necessary for any peace agreement.

British defence secretary Wes Streeting suggested the exercises forecast precisely such a scenario: “This isn’t a hypothetical plan, it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops.”

Zakharova, however, says that the exercises are “yet another confirmation that the Europeans have no place at the negotiating table”.

In the wake of Saturday’s deadly terrorist shooting in Kraków, a deputy defence minister has called for debate on limiting the number and types of weapons people can own. Meanwhile, a deputy interior minister says the tragedy provides an “incentive” to revisit proposals to better register certain guns.

Poland has among the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe, though the number of firearms licences being issued has risen in recent years and some politicians have called for expanded access to guns. Saturday’s attack was carried out by a man who legally owned firearms.

On Saturday, 24-year-old Michał Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, which was packed with tourists and locals, firing at random from his car.

He killed six people and injured over a dozen more. Later in the day, the bodies of the perpetrator’s parents and sister were found in his home, where they had been shot dead.

Oksiński’s rampage was brought to an end in a shootout with two police officers, which left all three with serious injuries. On Monday morning, the police announced that Oksiński had died in hospital. One of the police officers remains in what is described as “serious but stable” condition.

The man who carried out Saturday’s deadly terrorist attack in the Polish city of Kraków has died in hospital from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police.

One of the two officers who stopped him remains in serious but stable condition https://t.co/rT1YBXhkp7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 9, 2026

The incident has caused shock in Poland, a country that has never previously experienced this type of mass public shooting.

Speaking to Polsat News on Sunday, deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said that the tragedy “is the best illustration that it makes no sense to talk about expanding access to firearms”.

She added that “it’s already relatively easy” to obtain a gun licence, which can be granted to anyone aged 21 or over who has passed the relevant tests and declared that the firearm is for sporting purposes. Both Oksiński and his father had such licences and legally owned 11 firearms.

“I would like to start a discussion about whether access to such a large number of weapons should actually be so easy,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “This is also a question of whether someone who uses weapons for sporting purposes should have so many different types of weapons stored at home.”

 

Also speaking to Polsat on Sunday, Czesław Mroczek, a deputy interior minister, said that “weapons are certainly a challenge for us”. He noted that “in Poland we have had many cases of killings using black powder weapons, for which there is not even a register, let alone a permit procedure”.

Such weapons use traditional black powder rather than modern smokeless powder and include firearms manufactured before 1885 and their modern replicas.

According to a recent study by researchers from the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, they make up a considerable proportion of firearm-related fatalities in the country.

While noting that the issue is not directly related to the Kraków attacks, Mroczek said that plans to include these weapons in a register had already been drawn up and “this event [in Kraków] is an incentive for us to reexamine the matter”.

🇵🇱 Poland's interior ministry says black-powder guns, currently exempt from registration, will be entered into the register. The Krakow attack is described as an impulse to review the whole permit system.https://t.co/Nh7dr46MJ7

On Monday morning, the spokesman for the National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, held a press conference at which he provided further details on their findings so far.

He revealed that Oksiński had been found with two AR-15 rifles and two handguns on his person and in his car, as well as around 500 rounds of ammunition. He had earlier fired “several dozen, possibly several hundred, shots”.

A further seven guns had been found at Oksiński’s home. The total of 11 firearms matched the number of weapons there were permits for, noted Nowak, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska.

“The entire matter related to the weapons and the firearms permits will be reviewed,” added the spokesman. “We know that, since March of this year, he [Oksiński] has held firearms permits for one rifle and one pistol.”

Prosecutors have launched a terror investigation into Saturday’s shooting in Kraków, which left six dead. Three more bodies were later found in the suspect's home.

Further details have also emerged about the heroic actions of police and medical personnel https://t.co/icBJWLRK7c

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 8, 2026

Although gun ownership in Poland is relatively low, it has been rising steadily in recent years, particularly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with the total number of registered firearms owned by Poles surpassing 1 million, up from around 380,000 in 2014.

Last year, a record 50,709 new gun licences were issued in the country in 2025, up 10.6% compared to a year earlier.

Under Polish law, civilians can apply for licences for sporting, hunting, collecting and personal protection purposes. To obtain one, applicants must undergo medical examinations, pass a test, and join a relevant association, such as the Polish Sports Shooting Association, the Polish Hunting Association, or a collectors’ group.

Licences for sports and collection purposes are the most popular types of permits, together making up 76% of last year’s permits. But the number of licences issued for “personal protection” has grown from just 81 in 2021 to 7,254 last year.

A record 50,709 gun licences were issued in Poland last year and the total number of registered firearms has now surpassed 1 million.

Gun ownership in Poland has risen particularly rapidly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 https://t.co/axt2YS044Z

Access to firearms widened in 2023 under the former government, when parliament passed a law removing “unnecessary administrative and legal barriers.” That allowed members of uniformed services to apply for personal protection permits, a change lawmakers said was intended to “strengthen Poland’s defence potential”.

However, some politicians, especially on the right, have pushed for ownership rules to be further loosened. In September, speaking at the opening of a shooting range, President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, called for “public discussion about responsible access to weapons”.

“Even in the European Union, Poland remains at the bottom of the list in terms of access to firearms,” he said, quoted by Polsat. “Only about 1% of Polish citizens have access to weapons and are skilled at using them. Fortunately, I’m in that 1%.”

They were attending a “retreat and gala” hosted by CPAC, which also organises a major annual conservative political conference and has close ties to Trump. The cheapest tickets to attend the gala cost $2,500, ranging up to $7,500 for VIP access.

Blask Online’s photos show Ziobro eating dinner at the event and speaking to former British Prime Minister Liz Truss. Trump himself addressed the guests, saying that he “wants to congratulate everybody here”.

Ziobro is a deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, which is aligned with Trump and his Republican Party.

From 2015 to 2023, Ziobro served as justice minister in a PiS-led government, overseeing judicial reforms that are widely seen as having undermined the rule of law.

After a new, more liberal ruling coalition led by the current prime minister, Donald Tusk, took power in December 2023, it launched a number of investigations into the actions of senior PiS officials.

That led, last year, to prosecutors announcing that they want to charge Ziobro with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware, which was used to surveil some of PiS’s political opponents.

 

However, although parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution, he had by then already travelled to Hungary, which was at the time ruled by conservative PiS ally Viktor Orbán. In December 2025, the Hungarian government granted Ziobro political asylum.

At this year’s Hungarian parliamentary elections in April, Orbán’s Fidesz party was removed from power and his successor, Péter Magyar, pledged to extradite Ziobro to Poland.

The man who carried out Saturday’s deadly terrorist attack in the Polish city of Kraków – and who can now be named as 24-year-old Michał Oksiński – has died in hospital.

Oksiński suffered serious injuries in a firefight with two police officers, who heroically brought his rampage to an end. On Sunday, Krzysztof Klęczar, the governor of the Małopolska province in which Kraków is located, revealed that Oksiński remained in critical condition.

On Monday morning, provincial police announced that “the perpetrator of the tragic events [in Kraków] died this morning in hospital”.

“There was a constant struggle to save this man’s life, despite the evil he had committed,” Klęczar told broadcaster TVN after the death was confirmed. “He underwent at least three surgeries.”

Informujemy, że sprawca tragicznych wydarzeń zmarł dzisiaj nad ranem w szpitalu.

— Małopolska Policja (@kwpkrakow) November 9, 2026

The two police officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, who engaged Oksiński also suffered serious injuries, with Kulik’s condition the more critical of the two.

The situation would have been much worse were it not for the fact that two leading local surgeons had, by pure chance, been eating a meal with their families in a restaurant near where the shootout took place, and provided emergency aid to the officers.

There was also a huge public response to appeals for people to donate blood for Kulik, who underwent a series of surgeries.

On Sunday, it was announced that both Kulik and Morański had come out of the comas they had previously been placed in. Kulik’s condition was described as “serious but stable” by Karolina Gałecka, spokeswoman for the interior ministry.

CCTV footage shows the moment two police officers confront the Krakow shooter. pic.twitter.com/vcQ0Xvi1nX

— WarMonitor🇺🇦🇬🇧 (@WarMonitor3) November 7, 2026

Just after 3 p.m. local time on Saturday afternoon, Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, including its famous market square, which was packed with tourists and locals.

He fired at random from the car, killing six people. Four of those victims have been identified as Polish women, aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man in his 50s. The other two were foreign nationals: a 32-year-old British man and a 51-year-old Austrian woman.

A further 16 people were injured in the attack, 11 of them Polish. The interior ministry has said that, among the dead and injured are citizens of the UK, Austria, Germany, Russia and Portugal.

 

On Saturday evening, it was announced that a search of the perpetrator’s home in the small town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski in southeast Poland, around 160 km from Krakow, had revealed three further dead bodies.

They were later confirmed to belong to Oksiński’s parents, aged 53 and 52, and 21-year-old sister. Prosecutors believe Oksiński murdered them before launching his rampage in Kraków.

Oksiński’s motive remains unknown. On Saturday evening, in the wake of the attacks, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced at a press conference that the information obtained so far indicated that the suspect had “very, very radical views” and “may have been fascinated by far-right ideologies”.

However, when pressed on this claim during an interview with TVN on Sunday evening, Kierwiński refused to provide evidence, said that his remarks had referred to “initial hypotheses”, and confirmed that the potential motive was still being investigated.

Poland's interior minister refuses to reveal on what basis he said the Kraków terrorist had "very radical views" and was "fascinated by the far right".

"In cases like this, there are always first hypotheses, first clues. That's why I made this statement" pic.twitter.com/Wpud1FrAYM

— Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 8, 2026

The incident has caused shock in Poland, where gun crime is exceedingly rare. The country has one of the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe and has never previously suffered a mass public shooting of this kind.

In response to the tragedy, a period of two days of official public mourning has been declared, with a decree to that effect signed by President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk. On Monday evening, a silent march will be held in Kraków at 8 p.m. to pay tribute to the victims.

Legal giant Latham & Watkins, which generated $8.3bn (£6.3bn) last year, has launched a $1m (£760,000) programme to encourage associates to use AI.

The law firm said the financial rewards, which represent one per cent of the firm’s global revenue, will be awarded “to recognise associates who lead or materially contribute to AI initiatives that create value for clients, practice groups, matter teams or the firm as a whole.”

Latham & Watkins said individual awards “will vary based on the significance, impact, and scalability of each contribution.”

Michael Rubin, chair of Latham’s AI strategy committee, said the programme is part of the firm moving to “continue to advance our AI strategy”.

“Our associates bring firsthand insight into where AI can make a meaningful difference, and this award is designed to foster that ingenuity and help identify and scale the ideas that can create the greatest value for our clients and our firm,” Rubin said.

Latham said it will run a nomination process next spring to select the award recipients, with associates worldwide eligible.

Law firms look to reward AI use

Other law firms have followed similar financially based award incentives for AI use among younger members.

Shoosmiths, whose annual revenue was £221.4m, roughly 96 per cent less than Latham’s annual revenue, in April last year became the first major law firm to link a firmwide bonus to its workforce’s use of AI.

The firm exclusively told City AM that it set a “clear and ambitious annual target”: one million Microsoft Copilot prompts to unlock a £1m bonus pot for staff in the new financial year.

The City law firm doubled down on the commitment, setting aside a second £1m bonus pot after it hit the target four months early.

Before coming to power, the Labour Party promised to make the UK the fastest growing economy in the G7. Figures on Thursday morning suggested this pledge has been achieved, and ministers have rushed to take credit.

A year into government, modelled on China’s approach to business, the government published its industrial strategy. New statistics suggest that growth is broadly aligned with Labour’s apparent method of “picking winners” – to the detriment of some industries.

Labour officials had a Star Wars-sounding handle for its designated high-potential sectors: IS-8. It includes advanced manufacturing, clean energy, creative industries, defence, digital and technologies, financial services, life sciences, and professional and business services. 

Critics of the plan argued growth in the economy would not be organic. That, though, appears to be part of the point. Andy Burnham has doubled down his predecessor’s industrial strategy, highlighting the need for “good growth”, as opposed to any growth for the sake of growth. 

It raises the question of whether Whitehall officials tasked with boosting the government’s industrial strategy are also thinking on the kind of growth that ministers don’t want. 

In the last two years, official figures have broadly beaten market expectations. The UK economy accelerated in the third quarter of this year, hitting 0.7 per cent growth, despite predictions that the country was heading for a slowdown. Cue celebratory statements by Treasury ministers including Torsten Bell and Dan Tomlinson. Rachel Reeves, the former Chancellor, also offered her take on Thursday, praising “just how great a turnaround we achieved” in the economy.

Last week, the Bank of England said about a fifth of UK growth has been generated by AI-related investment. Bloomberg Economics thinks that about a fifth of growth has been driven by the ‘general purpose’ technology.

Official data showed that while growth of about 4.4 per cent in computer programming has helped boost the digital and technologies sector, the UK economy is benefitting from relatively strong performances across other parts of IS-8.

Some economists have suggested that added tax speculation before recent budgets have had upsides on growth in services after all, even it rumours cost the economy in other ways by prompting business owners to sell assets or pensioners to withdraw cash prematurely.

It’s not just professional and business services reaping the benefits of a government ready to back specific sectors. Equally significant, however, are the sectors which have suffered under Labour. Gambling and betting is one of the worst performing services sectors in the UK economy, after being hit with new taxes in Rachel Reeves’ 2025 Budget.

Charismatic leaders can be intoxicating, but Jensen Huang’s downfall exposes the peril of concentrating power, writes Dr Poornima Luthra

Many companies fall into the trap of placing excessive power and control in the hands of a few or even just one person. As we’ve seen with the recent scandal of the CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, who resigned today, this can be a dangerous strategy in a crisis. His affair with an alleged Chinese spy has led to company-wide reputational damage and consequent fall in share prices.

While ‘charismatic’ leaders can seem intoxicating – admired, respected and sometimes loved – this is a very dangerous hierarchy. When power is concentrated in one person there is a risk that their actions can negatively affect everyone else involved in a business, from employees to stakeholders. Huang’s predicament is a prime example, with a 30-year tenure as CEO, the ear of Donald Trump and a reputation for being workaholic who expects incredibly high standards from staff, his fall from grace is all the more damning.

Collective leadership shines in times of crisis

There is no denying the brand building prowess of a recognisable ‘face’, but strategic decisions should not depend on that individual alone. Collective and relational leadership offers far more resilience in the event of a crisis, with greater potential for maintaining trust and a general sense of ‘business as usual’. A key concern for investors going forward is that Nvidia has no clear succession plan for replacing Jensen Huang.

When I talk about ‘relational leadership’, I’m describing a democratic, team-based structure that creates a healthier culture, avoids cult-like devotion (and delusion) and generally ensures a business is more able to weather storms. Trust and relationships are central, arguably making ‘bad behaviour’ less appealing when there is a greater sense of shared goals and responsibilities. Building relationships also gives people space to excel and be themselves, while taking on a range of viewpoints that are so key to long-lasting success.

This trust is not just an internal sentiment; it is what ideally gets put out into the world to attract would-be customers. As Nvidia’s situation clearly demonstrates, trust can easily be undermined when the reputation of a business rests with an individual. Ultimately, leadership resilience is a fundamental aspect of good board governance and ensuring business continuity in the face of crisis. Many businesses think they might benefit from a single hero or charismatic leader, yet time and time again we see how this model exposes the organisation to immense risk.

Nvidia’s silver lining

Nvidia’s silver lining is the way their share holdings are structured. Unlike the likes of Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk, who have final say on board decisions thanks to significant ownership percentages in multiple types of stock, Nvidia’s shareholdings are built on a single class voting structure. That means there is only one type of stock for any investor in the company, including Huang, affording him no protections from actions of the board.

The lesson we can take from Nvidia is that the strength of an organisation should not depend on the popularity of the person at its head, but by the relationships and collective leadership that keep it sustained.

Dr Poornima Luthra is associate professor at Imperial Business School and author of Relational Leadership: How Trust, Collaboration, and Human Connection Drive High-Performance Organisations, out now, Thinkers50 Publishing

Lawyers and law firms will soon face increased fees to support the Solicitors Regulation Authority’s “transformation” strategy, as the regulator looks to reinvent itself following a string of high-profile corporate collapses in recent years.

As announced in its 2026-27 business plan, the regulator will increase its practising certificate price by over 26 per cent from £190 in 2025-26 to £240. The increase is expected to generate £111.5m. A qualified solicitor in England and Wales needs a practising certificate in order to provide legal services.

Since 2021-22, the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) has now increased the fees by more than 65 per cent from £145.

Its discretionary fund is seeing the largest jump in fees for both lawyers and law firms. The compensation fund is a safety net for clients, small businesses, charities, and trusts who suffer financial loss because a solicitor or law firm stole money or failed to account for money.

The fund has been forced to step in and support clients several times in recent years after a crop of corporate failures. Axiom Ince failed in 2023 when £64m of client money went missing, PM Law folded in February after a £39.5m suspected client-account fraud, and SSB Group collapsed in Janaury 2024 owing over £200m to litigation funders.

The SRA said on Thursday, as of 5 August, it had over 500 applications following the PM Law collapse, resulting in £15.6m being deducted from the fund.

The watchdog is set to increase its discretionary fund fees for solicitors from £70 to £170 and for law firms from £1,950 to £2,170, as the SRA said the “increase in contribution is required to meet its future obligations”. Since 2021-22, fees for lawyers have increased by 325 per cent, while fees for law firms have increased by over 185 per cent.

The SRA is also dealing with a rising tide of misconduct reports. Between November 2022 and October 2025, the number of misconduct reports it assessed rose by 45 per cent, from 11,378 to 16,499.

New boss orders regulatory ‘reset’

Sarah Rapson, SRA’s chief executive, has said it will be a complete regulatory “reset” of the watchdog.

“I was appointed chief executive in November 2025, at a time of growing pressure on the organisation. I spent my first months in the role carefully identifying issues and undertaking an evaluation of the areas that we need to address,” she said.

“While there is much the organisation does well and on which to build, the SRA faces multiple challenges which, taken together, mean that a reset is required.”

To maintain public confidence, the SRA said it is pushing forward with new rules that require firms to provide specific, binding timelines for resolution when a complaint is first made, along with a mandate to provide regular progress updates to the client.

The watchdog is narrowing its strategic focus to build a “wider menu of regulatory tools” designed to identify risks early. The plan outlined heavy investments in data collection and analysis to spot patterns of consumer harm and execute early interventions, rather than waiting to strike after a firm collapses.

Each week, we dig into the memory bank of the City’s great and good. Today, Mike Walters, CEO at Form3 and former Barclays big cheese, takes us through his career in finance, and the best advice he’s picked up in Square Mile and Me

CV

  • Name: Mike Walters
  • Job title: CEO at Form3
  • Previous roles: Chief product officer at Form3, product director at Barclaycard, head of payment product at Barclays
  • Age: 46
  • Born: UK
  • Lives: North Norfolk
  • Studied: LLB Law, MA Management
  • Talents: Running, woodwork
  • Motto: Go big or go home
  • Biggest perk of the job? People – I get to meet such a huge range of people all over the world.
  • Coffee order: Oat flat white
  • Cocktail order: Old fashioned
  • Favourite book: The Infinity Machine by Sebastian Mallaby

What was your first job?

I worked in an independent local camera shop – back when taking in films to process was most of the business!

What was your first role in the City?

I joined the Barclays Leadership Programme straight out of university. The first role for everyone was customer facing, which is a really good foundation. My clients were the largest UK companies, and I was there to help manage their relationship with the bank.

When did you know you wanted to build a career in business?

I’ve always been curious, and had worked out at school that one of the best ways to experience different industries would be accounting, law or management consultancy. I headed to uni to read law and very quickly realised that the piece that was most interesting was the corporate and commercial dimension of cases, rather than specifically looking at exactly how contracts might work! So I quickly moved to focus my studies on finance and banking. I joined the Barclays Leadership Programme, which I loved.

Over my time at Barclays I really enjoyed working with clients, matching what they needed with all the capabilities across the group globally. From there I moved from managing clients, to managing teams who managed clients, to managing and building payment products that all clients used, with an extremely tough period in 2008 managing relationships with North American financial institutions – probably one of the toughest and most tiring periods of my career.

In 2016 I co-founded Form3 to take all that experience and learning to build a payments tech company to serve banks and financial institutions around the world.

What’s one thing you love about the City of London?

Progress – everywhere you go, there is a real sense of moving forward but, balanced with a real sense of understanding and valuing the past. I really love that you can see new skyscrapers wrapped around buildings from 800 years ago. I think that’s a really powerful combination. Constantly driving forward is what helps our financial services industry to stand out on the world stage. I’ve definitely felt that as we’ve expanded into Europe and North America.

And one thing you would change?

Positivity. It’s so easy to think about problems, but the City is diverse, capable, experienced and innovative and we need to be proud of that, positive about that and get on with it.

What’s been your most memorable business lunch or meeting?

I always remember a first meeting with the corporate treasurer of a massive global business – he looked me straight in the eyes and said, “I will listen to any ideas you have where you are top three in the world, anything else don’t bother”. That has always stuck with me, be confident BUT really really understand why you are using people’s time, and think about it from their perspective. It was a little intimidating 12 months out of university!

And any business faux pas?

During my first interview event for a graduate programme, I’d never seen an office coffee dispenser before, one of those with a lever on the top. I was first to arrive at the interview and faffing around with how to make it work. I just pushed this lever on the top as hard as I could and it sprayed coffee literally all over the table and floor! I guess it made an impression at least.

What’s been your proudest moment?

At work, hands down seeing Form3’s platform cross through 10bn payments processed in our 10th year. It was such a monumental step in our journey, made up of so many important and proud moments along the way – but seeing that all come together and to see the business flying at scale like that was really a proud moment for me.

And who do you look up to?

Tough one, I’ve met some many amazing leaders, and many humble and talented people – I really try and find the skills and approaches that I love and weave them together.

What’s the best career advice you’ve ever been given?

Find the best people to work for, and hire people who are better than you.

And the worst?

I was once told “your team is there to make you look good”. I actually think the exact opposite is true – you are there to make your team look good, then anything is possible.

Are you optimistic for the year ahead?

YES! The world is not slowing down, but look, I wouldn’t be CEO of a proud, UK-founded tech company pushing out internationally if I didn’t see the amazing opportunities ahead of us. Of course there are challenges, and some are pretty daunting – let’s go after them.

We’re going for lunch, and you’re picking – where are we going?

I don’t get a lot of time for lunches, so we’re more likely to grab a soup / sandwich from Birleys.

And if we’re grabbing a drink after work?

Brewdog (love a good pint).

Where’s home during the week?

Flat by Liverpool Street Station.

And where might we find you at the weekend?

North Norfolk Coast – I’ve lived out that way with my family for years and absolutely love it. Fresh air, dark skies and fantastic pubs!

You’ve got a well-deserved two weeks off. Where are you going and who with?

A week with my wife and two kids, brain switched off in the sunshine (we love Croatia) and a week at home in Norfolk enjoying the space and taking on a woodworking project.

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. It can leave you speechless. It might stop you in your tracks and make you do a double take. The Christopher Ward C1 Bel Canto Lucia does all of the above.

This is a beautiful watch; no doubt about that, not beautiful as in a writer’s throwaway line, but beautiful as in stunning, the kind you need to see firsthand to confirm you were not dreaming.

The kind of watch you need to see on your wrist, the kind that makes you imagine how the light plays with the dial at different times of the day.

The kind of watch that finds you daydreaming, staring at its face and saying to yourself, “Man, that’s one fine watch”. The kind of watch you can lose your heart to, too.

Named after the lead character of Donizetti’s opera Lucia di Lammermoor, the Bel Canto Lucia takes inspiration from one of its most famous scenes, in which Lucia sings about a bird that only she can see.

The Bel Canto Lucia’s predecessor

The Bel Canto Lucia’s predecessor, the Christopher Ward C1 Bel Canto, showcased a chiming skeletonised complication. In a fortuitous twist of fate, admirers of that watch could not help but notice how the exposed hourly striking mechanism of the FS01 chiming module resembled a bird on the dial. And so a myth was born.

“People started pointing out very early on that FS01’s chiming works looked a bit like a bird. The slightly embarrassing truth is that this wasn’t necessarily intentional – the desired symmetry of the mechanism led us there,” says Christopher Ward Product Director Jörg Bader.

Bader goes on to explain, “With Lucia, Mr Jones Watches has taken that happy accident and turned it into something very real. The challenge for us was ensuring that the artwork could become part of the mechanism itself, with the beak and tail retaining genuine mechanical functions.”

The C1 Bel Canto Lucia follows in the footsteps of 2025’s C1 Celestial Moonphase, the first watch collaboration between Christopher Ward and Mr Jones Watches. Its 300-piece run sold out in less than 48 hours and was subsequently nominated at the Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG).

In light of its well-deserved success, talk turned to how the two companies could collaborate again, this time with a more technically ambitious brief: to integrate Mr Jones Watches’ artwork directly with the mechanical architecture of the watch.

On the Lucia, that resemblance to a bird is no longer left to one’s imagination. The mythical beast has become an integral working part of the watch, a songbird at its centre. The position of its beak tells you whether the chime is engaged: when the pusher at four o’clock is pressed, a delightful rotating bug mounted on the column wheel prompts the bird to open or close its beak.

Its tail has a rather more exciting job: for it is the hammer that delivers the hourly D note. It really is serendipity in motion.

“The Bel Canto watch was a dream to design for,” says illustrator and watch designer Andy Wilx. “I wanted to create a world you could peer into, and with so much space between the mechanism and crystal, I was able to create a design with real depth.”

Assembly

The bird isn’t simply painted onto the dial. It is assembled from six separate stamped brass pieces that travel to Mr Jones Watches, where each one undergoes a painstaking production process.

Here, the bird’s framing elements are gold-plated. The scene’s striking colours are applied using a traditional dial pad-printing process. Each and every colour requires its own printing plate and needs repeated applications to give Andy Wilx’s stunning design the grand treatment it deserves.

Layers and layers of ink are printed on an artwork measured in millimetres, as each of the 19 individual colours is laid down with the precision and dexterity that would make a heart surgeon proud.

I hold my hand up: two weeks ago I referenced the Hyrox founder’s ambition for his hybrid training venture to become part of the Olympics. Ended my sentence with a dot dot dot. Might as well have rolled my eyes. 

Within days, however, World Triathlon had announced that it was admitting Hyrox into its federation, and hence into the wider Olympic family, if not (at this stage) into the Olympics itself.

Details are sketchy for now. What’s in it for World Triathlon? Has money changed hands, or will it, in either direction? Has World Triathlon committed to lobby for Hyrox events to be part of Brisbane 2032 or a subsequent Games? 

If so, would WT be prepared for any of its existing Olympic disciplines to make way, or does it believe it could persuade the IOC to oust events from another sport with lesser appeal to younger generations?

Some elite triathletes have voiced concerns. Not every Hyrox adherent is overjoyed either – is courting the sporting establishment on brand?

“For us this is terrible… We’re still in for LA but who knows after that? It’s definitely concerning for the future of our sport and for the younger generations coming up,” triathlete Max Stapley told The Telegraph.

“We are paving the way for an entire generation of hybrid racers to chase their own Olympic dream,” says Moritz Furste, Hyrox co-founder.

Triathlon participation numbers around the world are well below their peaks. The sport – once a young challenger itself, only entering the Olympics at Sydney 2000 – caters increasingly to an older demographic.

While smaller in athlete numbers, Hyrox continues to grow apace with around 1.5m participants in the past year. It will need to demonstrate durable growth if it is to convince the International Olympic Committee of its merits. Only time will tell whether hitching its power sled to World Triathlon is the optimal way to do that given the obvious inter-discipline conflicts that will doubtless fester.

The IOC will decide on the Brisbane 2032 sport programme in April next year. A tight timeline for the newly married couple to work to.

Seems there’s no simple noun for a Hyrox athlete equivalent to triathlete. A void that needs filling, surely? Hyroxian, hyroxlete, hylete, hyroxter, hoxster, hyrocker?

Additionality

Every day is a school day. Mine on Monday was in the House of Lords where we launched a report on the social impact of wheelchair rugby and I learned about additionality. 

Primarily an economic term, in sporting studies it can refer to net social effects and is especially relevant to a sport such as ours which caters to individuals with often severe impairments and who might not otherwise be able to take part in any fitness activity at all.

The comparison we were asked to make by the report’s author was between his own sporting choices – if he wasn’t playing tennis he might well be on a golf course or a bike or out running – and those available to wheelchair users. 

Tennis could disappear and the net effect on the nation’s health, after a period of adjustment, might be slim. Remove wheelchair rugby and hundreds of players might fail to find an alternative physical and social outlet.

Parking for now my oft-mentioned scepticism about attributing hard financial value to society’s wellbeing, I am very pleased to relay that the analysis we commissioned shows an annual social value of £1,500 per GB Wheelchair Rugby member. And this is before what is earned as the positive “ripple effect” on players’ friends and families.

I mention all this because, like many disability sports, there is so much more we could do to grow the game and have this impact if we had more commercial partners alongside the excellent corporate supporters we have today. Please get in touch if you would like to learn more.

In the meantime, you can read our social impact report here.

Dawn of the Planet of the Apes

I ran around Battersea Park just after dawn yesterday morning and now know what it must be like to be a tailrunner. 

I was passed by scores of runners in both directions, most under half my age I guess, the males among them – who were firmly in the gender minority – trailing the odour of the previous evening’s Lynx in their wake.

Evidence of the continued Gen Z running boom, or instead were these healthy specimens all getting in their pre-work Hyrox training? The park’s 400m track appeared very busy, in spite of the early hour, as I peered through its chainlink surround. 8am reps? Probably confirms my hybrid suspicion.

Strangers on a train

Overheard on the train en route to Selhurst on Sunday.

Stranger #1: “I need to get out at the next stop. Where are you going?”

Stranger #2: “Going up to Twickenham. Just got a call to say my friend had a spare ticket for the rugby.”

Stranger #1: “That’s nice. I’ve never been. Is it league or union?”

Stranger #2: (Thinks for a long while) “Union, I guess.”

Hope #2 enjoyed the match. A man from Mars would surely be just as baffled at the existence of two rugby codes.

Glad all over (still)

Bottom of the league but you wouldn’t know it from the mood on my return journey from Selhurst. We Crystal Palace fans have often been here before. 

At the time of writing, manager Pierre Sage, much liked in the stands, is still in his job. My hope is that the club winning its first meaningful trophies in the past two seasons hasn’t hexed our recovery prospects. 

Never dull, always fun, wouldn’t have it any other way. Can they say that in the Stretford End?

Ed Warner is chair of Sussex Cricket and GB Wheelchair Rugby and writes his sport column at sportinc.substack.com

    Walking through the door of Number 10 Downing Street was one of the proudest moments of my life. I grew up in a council house, raised by a single mother, and never imagined I would one day be helping the Prime Minister tackle the cost-of-living crisis.

    It was an extraordinary privilege. Number 10 has an almost magical power to bring people together. Make a call from Downing Street and people answer. They listen. They want to help.

    But I also discovered something deeply frustrating. If you were designing an organisation to run a modern country, you wouldn’t design Number 10. The fragmentation, endless meetings and lack of accountability would be unthinkable in a successful business.

    I remember sitting through a roundtable involving 28 important people, including senior politicians and business leaders. Everyone had their say, then everyone went away. But I asked one simple question: what will be different tomorrow because we met today? The answer was virtually nothing.

    That experience crystallised a wider concern about how Britain is run. We have become a country that talks endlessly about growth while systematically discouraging the people who deliver it.

    And nowhere is that contradiction more damaging than in our attitude towards wealth creators.

    I helped build Just Eat from a struggling start-up into a business worth £5.5bn. We nearly went bust twice. We worked extraordinary hours, we took enormous risks and we created jobs in Britain – even when it might have made more financial sense to create them elsewhere.

    I am proud of that. Why shouldn’t I be? Yet increasingly, successful entrepreneurs are made to feel that their achievements are something to apologise for. When did ambition become a crime?

    The highest-earning one per cent of taxpayers contribute roughly a third of income tax revenues. The top 10 per cent contribute around 60 per cent. These are the people helping to fund our hospitals, schools, pensions and public services. So why are we sending them the message that we don’t particularly want them here?

    I work with investors and entrepreneurs who are genuinely relocating to Milan, Portugal and elsewhere. These aren’t theoretical threats, people really are leaving. And when they go, we don’t just lose their taxes. We lose their investment, their businesses, the salaries they pay and the opportunities they might have created for the next generation.

    Worse still, think what this tells a young person growing up in a council house today.

    My mother had a simple philosophy: no excuses. Work hard, take responsibility and get on with it. That mindset helped change my life. I want every young person in Britain to share that same self-belief, but instead, we’re creating a culture in which success is resented rather than celebrated, while too many young people are left without work, training or purpose.

    He arrived in Downing Street with enormous political capital, a fresh mandate for change and the ability to take difficult decisions. Yet his first Budget was painfully timid. A C-plus Budget when Britain needed something bold. He has talked about a ten-year economic plan, but any CEO will tell you that having a long-term vision is useless if you squander the moment when you have the power to deliver it.

    Worse, he looks to be continuing the very policies and attitudes that have driven Britain’s wealth creators away. A new leader cannot simply inherit a failed strategy and carry on implementing it. No successful business would tolerate that.

    Burnham is a good communicator. He should use that skill to win the argument for growth, not hide behind the manifesto of his predecessor. He should tell Britain that wealth creation is something to celebrate, not punish.

    And he should back those words with action. Make business investment fully tax-deductible. Stop penalising employers for creating jobs. Fix planning, accelerate energy connections and let businesses build.

    His message should be brutally simple: growth, growth, growth.

    Above all, he should start asking Britain’s most successful entrepreneurs a different question: what would persuade you to invest more here?

    Not how much more can we take from you. Not how can we make your life harder. But how can we help you create more jobs, more businesses and more prosperity?

    Because Britain doesn’t need fewer successful people. It desperately needs more.

    David Buttress is former CEO of Just Eat. Listen to him speak to Guto Harri and David Davis on their Politics Unleashed podcast

    Housing sales are forecast to have fallen to the lowest point in over three years as increased mortgage rates drive down buyer demand and the property market continues to cool.

    According to the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ (RICS) latest findings in its UK Residential Market Survey, the outlook for sales has slipped to the lowest point since July 2023, with October showing subdued demand and falling agreed sales.

    RICS said respondents to the survey “now expect both sales activity and prices to soften over the next twelve months.”

    The number of enquiries from new buyers has remained at the same level since September, with “virtually all parts of the UK reporting either falling or stagnant demand.”

    A decline in agreed sales worsened, falling to its lowest level in three months.

    Sales in the next twelve months are also expected to fall, which RICS said is “the most pessimistic assessment since July 2023.”

    London, East Anglia, the West Midlands and the South East recorded weaker housing price trends than the headline average.

    RICS Head of market research and analysis, Tarrant Parsons, said demand for buying houses “remains subdued” with respondents “bracing for a weaker year ahead for sales given the persistent macroeconomic challenges being faced.”

    Last week, the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee hiked interest rates for the first time since mid-2023, with policymakers warning another hike from the current four per cent was on the cards.

    “The Bank of England’s rate rise was accompanied by a clear warning that policy may need to tighten further if higher energy costs feed through into wider prices. With inflation now projected to approach five per cent next year, mortgage rates are likely to remain elevated for longer, thereby continuing to weigh on the market, Parsons said.

    Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, said the latest slump in buying confidence “shows how decisions in Washington not Westminster are shaping the outlook for the UK housing market.”

    He added that there “is growing pressure on Donald Trump to find a diplomatic solution following the mid-term elections, which means borrowing costs have started edging lower over the last week, a trend that would only accelerate if a lasting ceasefire was agreed.”

    James Cleverly, Festus Akinbusoye and Sara Gezdari are competing to be the Conservative candidate for Mayor of London. Here’s why that matters, according to Alys Denby

    Being a member of a political party may be a minority pursuit, but being a Conservative in London is something closer to masochism. The Party does not publish official figures but its membership is thought to be under 200,000, only a fraction of whom can plough their lonely furrow in this perennially Labour-voting city of 9m people. And this week, this hardy handful of souls is going to the ballot to pick their candidate for Mayor of London.

    They will choose between James Cleverly, Festus Akinbusoye and Sara Gezdari. The latter is the least well known, though she has previously run to be MP for Richmond Park. Her pitch is framed around her backstory as an immigrant from Albania. She recalls growing up in a collapsing economy with an AK-47 next to her bed. A bit like her leader Kemi Badenoch, she says that seeing what happens when savings evaporate along with the rule of law taught her the value of freedom, democracy and prosperity – and made her a Conservative. She wants to champion financial services to bring IPOs back to the stock exchange and has criticised the bank tax.

    Akinbusoye is a Westminster councillor and former police and crime commissioner for Bedfordshire. Unsurprisingly he cites “crushing crime” and restoring 40,000 police officers to the streets as a top priority, alongside being “pro-fun”. As a “fresh face” relatively untainted by the last Tory government, he believes he stands the best chance of winning under the alternative voting system.

    Experience and charisma

    By contrast, James Cleverly wants to use his parliamentary experience to his advantage. As a former foreign secretary, he says he knows how to promote the Capital to the world, as ex home secretary he understands the challenges of policing and immigration, and having run the Conservatives’ 2019 election campaign, he says he knows how to win. He’s a charismatic and recognisable figure who would use the platform of City Hall to challenge the government on anti-London measures like the so-called ‘mansion tax’ and ulez. When Burnham punishes success, Cleverly says, London pays.

    Whatever your politics, all Londoners should hope that Labour faces serious opposition at the upcoming Mayoral election. Sadiq Khan has failed this city – on house building, jobs, Tube strikes and more. He refuses to stand up to his own party as it seeks to siphon economic activity and influence away from the capital. London’s Conservatives bear a heavy responsibility, let’s hope they choose wisely.
