]]> NASA’s twin ESCAPADE spacecraft are on their way to Mars after successfully completing two unprecedented powered flybys of Earth, demonstrating a new approach that could allow future missions to launch without waiting for the usual two-year planetary alignment.

The spacecraft, named Blue and Gold, used a combination of Earth’s gravity and precisely timed engine burns on 7 and 9 November to accelerate towards the Red Planet. Both manoeuvres succeeded, putting the pair on course to reach Mars in September 2027.

The achievement completes the most demanding phase so far of an unusual journey that began almost a year ago.

“This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we’ve now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days,” said Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for NASA’s Heliophysics Division.

The mission, known as ESCAPADE (Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers), is led by the University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory. Its principal investigator, Robert Lillis, credited the operations team with successfully preparing both spacecraft for the critical manoeuvres.

“Our fantastic operations team put 110% into this critical manoeuvre, getting the spacecraft ready and watching like hawks for potential issues. We’re excited to now focus on our interplanetary journey. Onward, to Mars!” Lillis said.

Why NASA sent its Mars spacecraft back towards Earth

Most missions to Mars leave Earth during a relatively short launch window that opens roughly every 26 months, when the positions of the two planets allow spacecraft to make the journey with comparatively little fuel.

ESCAPADE took a different route. The two spacecraft launched aboard Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket from Cape Canaveral on 13 November 2025, when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun. Instead of heading directly towards Mars, they travelled towards a region around the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2, approximately one million miles from Earth.

They spent much of the following year following an elongated, looping trajectory that eventually brought them back towards our planet.

By the time they returned in November 2026, Earth and Mars had moved into a more favourable alignment.

The spacecraft then used Earth’s gravitational pull to change direction and gain speed. At the same time, each fired its engine for approximately nine minutes, providing the additional acceleration needed to begin the journey to Mars.

Blue completed its manoeuvre on 7 November at an altitude of approximately 1,000 miles above Earth. Gold followed two days later, passing about 650 miles above the planet.

The engine burns increased the spacecraft’s speed by more than 1,000 miles per hour.

The technique is known as a powered gravity assist, or Oberth manoeuvre. Although spacecraft have previously used planetary flybys to change their trajectories, NASA says this is the first successful use of a powered Earth flyby to send a mission towards Mars.

Jeff Parker of Advanced Space, the mission’s lead designer, said the approach could offer considerably more flexibility when planning future missions.

“With this loiter orbit and Earth flyby, ESCAPADE is pioneering a new strategy for getting to Mars,” Parker said.

“This method provides the flexibility to launch almost anytime and then use Earth’s gravity to get a boost to Mars, rather than waiting every two years to launch there directly when the planets are aligned.”

That flexibility could become important as more spacecraft are sent to Mars.

Launching during a narrow planetary window places considerable demands on launch facilities, spacecraft preparation and mission schedules. Weather problems or technical delays can cause missions to miss their opportunity and wait another two years.

ESCAPADE has demonstrated that spacecraft can launch earlier, remain in a suitable orbit and depart for Mars when the planetary positions become favourable.

Mark Lewis, manager of Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory Mission Operations Center, said the successful manoeuvres could change how missions are scheduled.

“It would open up the possibility for people to launch in between transfer windows, loiter around, and then go when it’s convenient to do so,” he said.

The approach does not eliminate the importance of planetary alignment for the journey to Mars. Instead, it separates the initial launch from Earth from the spacecraft’s eventual departure towards the planet.

Two spacecraft will investigate why Mars lost its atmosphere

Once at Mars, ESCAPADE’s two spacecraft will investigate how the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun, interacts with the planet’s magnetic environment and contributes to the loss of its atmosphere.

Mars once had rivers, lakes and a much thicker atmosphere. Today, its atmosphere is less than 1% as dense as Earth’s. The planet no longer has a global magnetic field, although magnetised rocks in its crust produce localised fields. Scientists believe the solar wind has played a significant role in stripping away atmospheric gases over billions of years.

NASA’s MAVEN spacecraft has already studied this process, but ESCAPADE will provide something different: two spacecraft making coordinated observations of the same changing environment.

This will help scientists distinguish changes occurring over time from differences between locations, something that is difficult to establish using measurements from a single orbiter.

“This will be the first science mission to choreograph two orbiters around Mars, and the first time we will be able to make coordinated observations of the Martian environment from two different locations simultaneously,” said Robert Lillis, ESCAPADE’s principal investigator at UC Berkeley.

“The formation flying will allow us to investigate how the dynamic Martian magnetosphere varies both spatially and temporally.”

Blue and Gold are scheduled to enter Martian orbit on 7 and 9 September 2027, respectively. Each will fire its engine for approximately 11 minutes to slow down and enter orbit.

Science operations are expected to begin in June 2028, following several months of orbital adjustments. The spacecraft will initially follow one another in the same orbit, allowing researchers to measure how conditions change over short periods.

Six months later, they will move into separate orbits. One will travel farther from Mars to monitor the incoming solar wind, while the other remains closer to the planet to observe its effects. The arrangement will allow scientists to compare the solar wind with the planet’s response at nearly the same time.

What the mission means for astronauts on Mars

The research has implications beyond understanding the planet’s ancient climate.

Mars has little protection from the radiation associated with solar storms, making space weather an important consideration for future astronauts living or working on its surface.

ESCAPADE’s measurements could help scientists better understand how energetic particles behave around Mars and improve the information needed to assess radiation hazards.

“We will be making the space weather measurements we need to understand the system well enough to forecast solar storms whose radiation could harm astronauts on the surface of Mars or in orbit,” Lillis said in an earlier UC Berkeley account of the mission.

The Martian ionosphere, a region of the upper atmosphere containing electrically charged particles, is another area of interest.

Changes in this region can affect radio signals, potentially complicating communications and navigation for spacecraft, aircraft and people operating on Mars.

“Understanding how the ionosphere varies will be a really important part of understanding how to correct the distortions in radio signals that we will need to communicate with each other and to navigate on Mars,” Lillis said.

Michele Cash, ESCAPADE programme scientist at NASA Headquarters, said the mission could help prepare for future human exploration.

“By better understanding how the solar wind affects the Martian environment, ESCAPADE’s findings could help us plan and prepare for future human exploration of the Red Planet,” she said.

A smaller, lower-cost approach to planetary exploration

ESCAPADE is also testing a different model for conducting planetary science.

The mission is part of NASA’s Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration, or SIMPLEx, programme, which supports lower-cost missions that accept greater technical risk than traditional large planetary spacecraft.

UC Berkeley leads the project, with Rocket Lab responsible for building the two spacecraft. Other partners include NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Advanced Space and Blue Origin.

Berkeley’s scientific instruments include devices that measure charged particles escaping from Mars, while other instruments examine magnetic fields and plasma surrounding the spacecraft.

The mission’s scientific objectives build on decades of observations by previous Mars orbiters, but its two-spacecraft arrangement offers a capability those missions did not have.

ESCAPADE has already begun collecting useful measurements during its journey.

While travelling through its extended orbit around Earth, the spacecraft passed through distant regions of Earth’s magnetotail, the elongated part of our planet’s magnetic environment that stretches away from the Sun.

Scientists have collected observations of the structure and behaviour of that region and expect to continue studying the solar wind during the 10-month cruise to Mars.

As Lillis observed while discussing the difficulties of eventually establishing a human settlement on Mars, the challenges remain formidable.

“It is definitely going to be a challenge to establish a human settlement on Mars,” he said. “But, you know, humans are tenacious, right?”

]]> Virgin Atlantic’s Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Corneel Koster has called on the UK government to “take a closer look” at London Heathrow Airport’s decision-making following recently announced plans to redistribute airlines across its terminals. The decision sees Virgin Atlantic being separated from joint venture partner Delta Air Lines which would move from terminal 3 to terminal 4.

Virgin founder Richard Branson previously deemed the move “short-sighted” and urged the airport to reverse its plan which would come into effect in 2028. The company is Heathrow’s second-largest carrier after British Airways which is unaffected by these changes.

Virgin Atlantic encourages government to “take a closer look”

“We would urge the government to take a closer look at this,” Koster told the Airlines 2026 conference in London on Wednesday. He argued that this was no longer a reasonable commercial discussion with the airport.

“Heathrow refuses to engage commercially,” he added. “If you know Virgin Atlantic, we’re not going to sit quietly between a rock and a hard place. We’re going to challenge this extremely hard.”

“There is no way that we will ever accept this,” Koster said, referring to Virgin Atlantic and Delta Air Lines.

Koster pointed to the government’s care towards the cost of living crisis, highlighting how Heathrow’s move is “anticompetitive” and would cause an increase in fares. “It’s completely anti-competitive. It’s mindless. It’s irrational.”

He noted the importance of connecting traffic for which the Delta-Virgin joint venture provides, particularly on the US-Africa/Asia markets and vice-versa.

His calculations suggest that the entry of Virgin Atlantic on routes otherwise operated solely by British Airways pushes fares down by 16% on average, and up to 21% in economy class.

A drop in feeder traffic through its Delta Air Lines partnership may mean that “not all routes will be viable,” he warned.

Making connections via Heathrow harder

Separating Delta and Virgin has a considerable impact on journey times, commercial viability of certain connections and customer experience. Koster described T4’s remoteness as the “worst of all worlds”.

Delta previously operated out of T4 until 2016 when it shifted to T3 as it further integrated its operation with that of Virgin.

When the changes come into effect, passengers transiting between a Delta and Virgin flight will need to clear security and wait for a bus to change terminals. “Our connecting times will at least increase by 50%,” Koster calculates. At a minimum, the terminal change will require connecting times to be 90 minutes.

Koster worries that the changes will make the Virgin-Delta proposition less attractive to consumers who would instead be inclined to fly with the competition.

“No hub in the world would ever propose to split a joint venture, certainly not a joint venture with a home-based airline like ourselves. It’s outrageous, quite frankly.”

Virgin Atlantic proposed alternatives

The main objective for London Heathrow’s changes is to ensure the existing capacity is utilised efficiently. There remains underutilised space in terminal 4, prompting airline occupancy adjustments from the operator. The process has been ongoing for several years, with effect from 2028.

Virgin Atlantic proposed several “credible” alternatives. “The optimal alternative was for SkyTeam to be co-located in terminal 2,” he told Airlines 2026. That terminal is currently used by Star Alliance member airlines.

SkyTeam connects double the number of passengers than Star Alliance at Heathrow, the CEO underlined.

The other option the airline proposed was to move other airlines out of terminal 3 that were “not as integrated as the joint venture”. Other carriers that use T3 include Sri Lankan Airlines, Hainan Airlines, Emirates, Cathay Pacific, LATAM and Aeromexico to name a few.

Heathrow’s capacity constraints limit the operator’s flexibility

Responding to some of Koster’s remarks, Thomas Woldbye CEO of Heathrow Airport took to the stage in the afternoon to address the conference. “We’re not happy when they’re not happy,” he began, referring to his customers.

He deemed the alternatives as “expensive” adding that moving more airlines would be too cumbersome. Action had to be taken, Woldbye said, as it is their “legal and regulatory obligation” to use all remaining capacity. “We cannot sit and not take the decisions.”

He noted that these “marginal decisions” related to airline terminal occupancy were needed in the absence of a third runway. When asked whether Virgin and Delta would be put back together once built, he said:  “I think that would definitely be the case.”

Virgin Atlantic (similarly to British Airways) has backed the construction of a third runway so long as the price is right.

“If you then look at expansion, they want to spend eye-watering amounts with guaranteed returns on expansion,” Koster said. “We’re all for expansion. We absolutely need expansion with Heathrow, but we need it to be done in an affordable way.”

]]> Greece is expanding its fleet of V-BAT surveillance drones for the Hellenic Army and Navy under a new order placed through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), giving its armed forces more aircraft capable of operating from ships, islands and remote coastal positions without runways.

US defence technology company Shield AI announced the agreement on 11 November, saying the additional aircraft would strengthen intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) operations on land and at sea.

The contract includes spare parts, training, ground support equipment and long-term maintenance support. Shield did not disclose the number of aircraft ordered, their cost or the delivery schedule.

The latest procurement expands an existing Greek military capability and comes as Shield develops partnerships with Greek companies covering autonomous flight software, drone interceptors and future unmanned combat aircraft.

Why Greece needs runway-independent drones

The V-BAT is designed to operate from confined spaces, including small ship decks and remote military positions.

Unlike conventional fixed-wing drones, which generally require runways or launching equipment, V-BAT takes off and lands vertically. Once airborne, it transitions into forward flight using its wings.

This allows military units to deploy the aircraft from locations where conventional surveillance drones would be difficult to operate.

Shield says V-BAT can remain airborne for more than 12 hours, providing extended surveillance without requiring a large aircraft or airfield.

The capability is particularly relevant to the Aegean, where Greece maintains military positions across numerous islands and coastal areas.

“An order for additional V-BATs represents a major expansion of Greece’s persistent ISR capacity and a strong vote of confidence in an aircraft already operating in Hellenic service,” said James Lythgoe, Shield’s regional director for Eastern and Southeast Europe.

He said the common fleet would allow the Army and Navy to share training, logistics and operational experience.

“V-BAT is exceptionally well suited to the Aegean, where forces need long-endurance ISR from islands, coastlines, ships and austere sites without dependence on runways.”

How the V-BAT works

V-BAT is a Group 3 unmanned aircraft powered by a heavy-fuel engine.

Its distinctive feature is a single ducted fan, with the propeller enclosed inside a circular housing at the rear of the aircraft.

The drone stands vertically during takeoff and landing before moving into conventional wing-borne flight.

It can carry surveillance equipment to observe and track activity on land or at sea. Shield lists a maximum payload capacity of 40lb (18kg).

The company says V-BAT has demonstrated the ability to operate in environments where GPS signals are disrupted or communications are contested.

Such capabilities have become increasingly important as electronic warfare systems are used to interfere with drone navigation and control.

Greece develops its own autonomous capabilities

The latest order follows a strategic agreement signed by Shield and Greece’s EFA GROUP at the Eurosatory defence exhibition in Paris on 16 June.

The companies agreed to develop and integrate artificial intelligence-based pilots for unmanned systems using Shield’s Hivemind autonomy software.

Hivemind is designed to allow an aircraft to respond to changing conditions, alter its route and avoid obstacles without requiring continuous instructions from a human operator.

Unlike a conventional autopilot that follows a programmed route, the software can adapt its actions within parameters established by military operators.

Under the agreement, EFA GROUP will contribute engineering and systems integration expertise to adapt the technology to Greek requirements.

The companies say the arrangement is intended to give Greece greater national control over autonomous military capabilities, including their long-term maintenance and development.

“By combining Shield AI’s proven autonomy stack with EFA GROUP’s engineering, this partnership creates a pathway for next-generation solutions developed in country, as envisioned in Agenda 2030, both for Greece and Europe,” said Dr Grigoris Koutsogiannis, CEO of EFA GROUP, when the agreement was announced.

The companies have not confirmed that the additional V-BAT aircraft ordered through NSPA will incorporate technology developed under this partnership.

More defence cooperation with Greek industry

Shield has announced two other agreements with Greek companies this year.

In July, it partnered with ALTUS LSA to integrate the Greek-built KMB Hunter interceptor with V-BAT, potentially giving the aircraft a role in counter-drone operations.

In October, Shield signed a memorandum of understanding with GEK TERNA to explore opportunities involving its larger X-BAT unmanned combat aircraft, including potential local production and maintenance.

X-BAT is a separate vertical takeoff and landing aircraft being developed for combat missions.

The company has also opened a regional office in Athens.

NATO agency handles procurement and support

The new V-BAT order was placed under NSPA’s Uncrewed Aerial Systems Support Partnership, which allows participating countries to acquire aircraft and support services through a common framework.

The agency provides assistance covering procurement, spare parts, maintenance, training and technical support. Greece retains ownership and operational control of its aircraft.

Shield is also expanding V-BAT sales outside Europe. In January, the company announced that the Indian Army had selected the aircraft alongside licences for its Hivemind software.

The latest Greek order adds to that international business while extending the country’s existing surveillance capability across its Army and Navy.

]]> Russia reportedly lost three military aircraft and seven crew members while attempting to repel a Ukrainian drone attack near St. Petersburg, with Russian military aviation channels mourning fatalities and conflicting accounts emerging over which aircraft were involved.

The reported losses came during an overnight assault on November 10–11 that also triggered fires at Ust-Luga, a major Russian Baltic Sea export hub. Neither the full aircraft tally nor the circumstances of the reported crashes have been independently confirmed.

Russian accounts have pointed to Ka-52 attack helicopters and a Mi-8 transport helicopter. Other reports identify a MiG-31 interceptor among the losses, although the aircraft types remain disputed.

The pro-war Fighterbomber Telegram channel said defending the skies over St. Petersburg had cost Russia “very, very, very dearly,” posting a tribute to fallen aviators.

Russian aviation channels mourn crews after St. Petersburg drone attack

Ukraine’s overnight attack on November 10–11 targeted Ust-Luga, one of Russia’s main Baltic Sea export hubs. Footage showed fires at the port, while NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-monitoring system detected hotspots in the area.

Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) also said its drones struck the Naro-Fominsk, a Buyan-M-class missile corvette. The extent of the reported damage to the vessel has not been independently confirmed.

Reports of Russian aviation losses emerged after the pro-war Fighterbomber Telegram channel posted a tribute to fallen aircrew.

“Today’s defense of the skies over St. Petersburg against a drone attack has cost us dearly. Very, very, very dearly. May you fly eternally, brothers…” the channel wrote.

Fighterbomber is associated with Ilya Tumanov, a former Russian military aviator whose channel frequently reports on the country’s air force. His post did not identify the aircraft involved or explain how the crews died.

Other Russian aviation channels subsequently published tributes, including an image of a Ka-52 attack helicopter. The Voevoda Veshchaet channel reported the deaths of three crews, totalling seven personnel.

Which Russian aircraft were reportedly lost?

The aircraft types remain disputed. Reports have named Ka-52 attack helicopters and a Mi-8 transport helicopter, while other accounts have included a MiG-31 interceptor.

Ukrainian defence publication Militarnyi, drawing on Russian Telegram channels, assessed that the losses likely involved two Ka-52s and one Mi-8. That combination would account for seven crew members: two aboard each Ka-52 and three aboard the Mi-8.

⚡️❗️It seems we finally know which three Russian aircraft were lost over Leningrad Oblast while repelling today’s Ukrainian drone attack: Ka-52 — 2 crew members Mi-8 — 3 crew members MiG-31 — 2 crew members All seven crew members died. The more details emerge, the more baffling this incident becomes. How did Russia manage to lose three aircraft at the same time during a drone attack, and how did every single crew member aboard all three aircraft end up dead?

— Special Kherson Cat 🐈🇺🇦 (@bayraktar_1love) November 11, 2026

A different breakdown circulated by Ukrainian open-source intelligence account Special Kherson Cat identified one Ka-52, one Mi-8 and one MiG-31. That would also total seven crew members, meaning the reported death toll alone cannot resolve the conflicting aircraft identifications.

Russia’s Defense Ministry has not confirmed the reported aircraft losses. The SBU, meanwhile, said information about the destruction of Russian combat helicopters was being verified.

AGN has previously reported on Russia’s use of aircraft and helicopters to intercept Ukrainian long-range drones. Such missions extend the demands on Russian aviation beyond operations near the front, requiring crews and aircraft to defend infrastructure deep inside the country.

If confirmed, the loss of three aircraft and their crews during a single overnight drone attack would underline the risks involved in those defensive missions. It would not, by itself, establish that Ukrainian drones directly shot them down.

“Just get in range and shoot”: Ukraine’s F-16s claim 4,700 drone kills “Just get in range and shoot”: Ukraine’s F-16s claim 4,700 drone kills

What caused the reported Russian aircraft losses?

The circumstances remain unclear. Russian military bloggers have discussed possible friendly fire or a collision, but no publicly verified evidence establishes what happened.

In its November 11 assessment, the Institute for the Study of War said it had not observed footage of the alleged incidents or information confirming the total number of helicopters lost. Ukraine’s Security Service also said information about the destruction of Russian combat helicopters was being verified.

]]> £5.7B easyJet buyout gets shareholder greenlight as CEO hails win for passengers and staff https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/easyjet-apollo-shareholder-greenlight/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:42:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56440 The deal is expected to be completed before the end of the first calendar quarter of 2027, the company said in a release.

The post £5.7B easyJet buyout gets shareholder greenlight as CEO hails win for passengers and staff appeared first on AGN.

]]> On Wednesday morning, 11 November, easyJet announced that its shareholders had approved a plan for Apollo Global Management, an American asset and private equity firm, to takeover the company in a deal worth £5.7 billion.

The deal –which will be one of the largest of its kind involving the private equity acquisition of a European airline– is expected to be completed before the end of the first calendar quarter of 2027.

The takeover was approved by a large majority of the company’s shareholders. This will ultimately mean that easyJet exits the London stock market once completed. According to its official documents, 35% of the company’s shares are owned by EU nationals.

easyJet says this will benefit passengers

At the Airlines 2026 conference held in London on Wednesday, easyJet CEO Kenton Jarvis said that the deal was a “very good thing” for passengers.

“We’ve obviously spoken to Apollo and it’s clear that they support the strategy that we have and see great opportunities to accelerate it.”

He added that the carriers’ core ethos will remain intact. “When we think about our strategy and our purpose of making low-cost travel easy, affordable and accessible for as many people as possible, then that will remain the purpose of easyJet, and we will look to provide the products and the services that our customers value.”

Jarvis added that the deal was both exciting and “good for the future.”

Discover: Who is easyJet’s buyer Apollo? Discover: Who is easyJet’s buyer Apollo?

Obtaining regulatory approval

A primary hurdle for the deal is regulatory compliance. easyJet holds several Air Operators Certificates (AOCs) across Europe, including in the UK, Austria and Switzerland. As such, it will need to obtain regulatory approval from the Civil Aviation Authorities in each of these countries.

The company has also had to submit competition filings, which Jarvis explains have been progressing well. “A lot of those are starting to come through now: approved, approved, approved,” he said.

“We haven’t had an issue with competition filings because Apollo doesn’t own any airlines in Europe, and therefore there’s no real change in terms of the landscape. So it’s down for the regulators.

Disquiet from trade unions

The deal has faced criticism from trade unions, with the European Works Council –that represents the airline’s employees across Europe– warning that it would weaken the company’s long-term resilience.

But Jarvis believes the agreement brings plenty of good.

“I think for the staff it’s a very positive thing because it’s a positive thing for the company.”

He added that many of the staff are also shareholders, who voted in Wednesday’s meeting to approve the takeover.

“It’s very good for us because we can continue to grow and look to execute in our strategy.”

Will Apollo’s takeover result in a new strategy for easyJet?

Apollo has previously outlined its broad plans for easyJet following its acquisition. It hopes to continue the airline’s fleet modernisation and expansion plans, enhance its ancillary and loyalty offerings and scale its Holidays business.

Jarvis reiterated these elements on Wednesday, boasting the carrier’s “strong” and “flexible” orderbook, including the introduction of additional A320 family jets to replace its older A319s. The company has previously said it hopes to withdraw the smaller jets from its fleet by 2030.

“That gives great benefits in terms of not only the environment and the carbon footprint, but also the cost of operating those aircraft and then that will give good value to the customer,” he said.

The carrier will also launch a new loyalty programme next year. It currently offers its easyJet Plus scheme, which passengers can buy into to take advantage of a range of perks including free carry-on bags, fast-track security and extra-legroom seats.

The new programme will “help deepen engagement with our customers and also reward our customers for their loyalty, which is great.”

He adds that the easyJet Holidays offering continues to grow.

]]> Magnifica Air confirmed as buyer of 10 Airbus A220 corporate jets https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/magnifica-air-10-airbus-a220-corporate-jets/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:08:17 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56466 Airbus has identified Magnifica Air as the customer behind an existing firm order for 10 ACJ220-300 aircraft. The Florida-based premium airline plans a 17-aircraft fleet.

The post Magnifica Air confirmed as buyer of 10 Airbus A220 corporate jets appeared first on AGN.

]]> Magnifica Air has been identified as the customer for a previously undisclosed order for 10 Airbus ACJ220-300 aircraft. The new aircraft would expand the Florida-based premium airline’s planned fleet to 17 jets as it prepares to launch operations in 2028.

Airbus Corporate Jets disclosed the customer on 10 November. The airline’s planned fleet comprises 14 ACJ220 aircraft and three ACJ321neos. 

Magnifica intends to use the jets for scheduled premium services combining low-density cabins with elements of private aviation, including dedicated terminals, ground transfers and concierge assistance.

Magnifica plans 54-seat A220 cabins

The newly disclosed ACJ220-300 aircraft will carry 54 passengers, including accommodation in a private suite, according to Corporate Jet Investor. A typical airline-configured A220-300 carries about 150 passengers, but Magnifica has significantly reduced the seat density for its all-premium service.

The A220-300 is the larger member of Airbus’s A220 family, not to be confused with the ACJ TwoTwenty corporate jet, which is derived from the smaller A220-100. The airline’s larger corporate jets would support its scheduled passenger operations.

Airbus says the ACJ220-300 can fly up to 4,000 nautical miles in a full business-class configuration. Actual range will depend on cabin fit-out, payload and operating conditions. The airline has previously identified major US cities and selected leisure destinations as potential markets for its ‘Private Class’ service.

Magnifica picks Skywise digital solutions to manage operations

Alongside the aircraft order, Magnifica selected Airbus’s Skywise digital solutions, including Skywise Core X1, flight planning, operations and crew management tools, and navigation databases. The systems would support flight and technical operations as the airline builds its fleet.

“Airbus is far more than an aircraft manufacturer. They understand high-end travel and where the business aviation travel market is going. From our first conversations, their team recognised what we set out to build: Private Class, a new category of flight, built on one principle: Beknown. From the first call to the final arrival, every detail is shaped around the individual travel experience. Our ACJ fleet is a critical part of delivering the Private Class experience. The ACJ220-300, together with Skywise, gives us the cabin, the range and the operational backbone to bring it to our members,” said Wade Black, CEO of Magnifica Air, in the announcement. 

Airbus Corporate Jets president Chadi Saade said: “The ACJ220-300 is the perfect fit for Magnifica Air’s disruptive model, offering unrivalled cabin space and intercontinental range with significantly lower operating costs. By selecting the ACJ220-300, Magnifica Air is securing the most efficient and comfortable aircraft in its class that perfectly suits their innovative business model to get its customers in the most efficient way where it matters, when it matters.”

Cabin completion and aircraft deliveries remain to be clarified

Magnifica previously selected Comlux for cabin completion work on aircraft in its initial fleet. However, Corporate Jet Investor reports that the airline is issuing a request for proposals for the interiors of the 10 newly identified ACJ220-300s. The contractor for that work has not yet been confirmed.

The publication also reports that the company’s first A220-300 is in production. Airbus and Magnifica have not announced a delivery timetable for the 10 aircraft, or when they are expected to enter service.

The aircraft order is a significant commitment for an airline that has yet to begin scheduled services. Magnifica’s model depends on attracting passengers willing to pay for a more private travel experience while profitably operating aircraft with far fewer seats.

Magnifica has revised its intended launch from 2027 to 2028, according to a clarification the airline’s press representative provided to Aerospace Global News in earlier reporting. The timing of aircraft deliveries, cabin completion and regulatory preparations will be central to meeting that revised target.

Aerospace Global News has reached out to Magnifica Air to confirm the completion arrangements and delivery schedule.

 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: 800px;}
.sie-dest-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 19px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: 1100px;
 line-height: 1.5;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 15px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-dest-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);
 color: #fff;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;
 color: #fff;}
.sie-country-heart--hero{position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 padding: 10px 20px;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 gap: 8px;
 border-radius: 6px;
 min-width: unset;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.92);
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);
 box-shadow: none;
 backdrop-filter: none;
 white-space: nowrap;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-family: inherit;
 line-height: 1;
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;}
.sie-country-heart--hero:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.22) !important;
 border-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.9) !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 transform: none;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.voted{background: rgba(239, 68, 68, 0.28) !important;
 border-color: #f87171 !important;
 color: #fff !important;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.voted i{color: #fca5a5;}
.sie-country-heart--hero .sie-country-heart__count{display: none;
 font-size: 12px;
 opacity: 0.85;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count{display: inline;}
.sie-dest-body{max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-dest-stats{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 10px;
 margin: 32px 0;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-dest-stat{flex: 1;
 min-width: 150px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 18px 20px;
 border-right: 1px solid #d4e0f5;}
.sie-dest-stat:last-child{border-right: none;}
.sie-dest-stat__label{font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 600;
 color: #505a6b; 
 text-transform: uppercase;
 letter-spacing: 0.06em;}
.sie-dest-stat__value{font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #003B73;
 line-height: 1.3;}
.sie-admreq-cta-strip .sie-dest-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 0.5rem;
 padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
 background: #fff;
 color: #1d4ed8;
 border-radius: 6px;
 font-weight: 700;
 text-decoration: none;
 font-size: 0.97rem;
 transition: opacity 0.2s;}
.sie-admreq-cta-strip .sie-dest-hero__cta:hover{opacity: 0.9;}

 /* ── Make the search the priority, not an afterthought ────────────────
 Measured before this change at 1440x900: hero 1028px tall, search bar
 top at y=694. Tightened the vertical rhythm and moved the trust row
 below, which lifts the bar roughly 230px — comfortably in view. */
 .lh-hero.lh-hero{padding:clamp(28px,4vw,56px) 0 clamp(32px,4.5vw,64px)}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{gap:clamp(16px,2vw,26px)}
 /* ⚠️ THE CAUSE OF THE BIG EMPTY GAP, and it was mine. The stylesheet sets
 .lh-hero-text{flex:1 1 380px} and .lh-portals{flex:1 1 420px}. Those were
 written for the original ROW layout, where flex-basis is a WIDTH. Turning
 the container into a column silently turned both into fixed HEIGHTS: the
 text box stayed 380px tall although its content ended after 187px, and
 the search row stayed 420px tall although the cards are 195px. That is
 ~420px of enforced emptiness. Resetting the basis is the whole fix —
 never set flex-direction on an inherited flex container without checking
 what flex-basis meant before. */
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{margin-bottom:10px}

 /* ── Results as a responsive grid, not a single strip ──────────────────
 .sie-res-list holds the program cards as direct children (verified live:
 18 cards, one parent, no headers in between), so one grid rule is enough.
 ⚠️ SCOPED TO THE HOMEPAGE ON PURPOSE. .sie-res-list is the shared
 SieFlowView markup — Leonardo renders into it too, with its own
 per-card animation offsets. Re-layouting it globally would change his
 results as a side effect of a homepage fix. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(320px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list > .program-card{width:auto;max-width:none;margin:0}

 per country. Each branch carries max-width:560px inside a 798px rail, so
 two never fit and they stack — the "single strip". Releasing the cap and
 tiling the branches gives two country panels per row at this width, and
 more on a wider screen, without touching the cards inside.
 ⚠️ Scoped to .lh-herosearch: Leonardo renders the same flow markup. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(360px,1fr));gap:18px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branch{max-width:none;width:100%}
 /* ── The figures strip ────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Serif numerals, monospaced labels, hairline rules, no card, no shadow,
 no colour fill behind each figure. The register of a register. */
 .lh-stats.lh-stats--figures{background:#F4F2ED;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-bottom:1px solid #E4E0D8;padding:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:0 clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}
 /* Every cell except the first gets inner space on its left, so each rule
 sits with equal air on both sides instead of crowding the next figure.

 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat + .lh-stat{padding-left:clamp(18px,2.4vw,34px)}

 /* #6B7A8D measured 3.92:1 against the warm band — under the 4.5:1 that
 11.5px text needs. The cool grey was fine on the old cold background and
 quietly failed when the palette warmed up; #4F5967 measures 6.2:1.
 Worth remembering when warming any other background. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}

 .lh-inst-body{margin:0 0 26px;font-size:clamp(15.5px,1.4vw,17px);line-height:1.65;color:#C6D2E0;max-width:54ch}

 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────
 Brings the sections below the hero onto the palette and type the hero
 already uses, so the page reads as one document instead of two designs
 stacked on top of each other. Everything here is homepage-only (it lives
 in this template) and is pure CSS: delete this block to revert. */
 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which
 showed through every transparent section (the institutions carousel and
 the study fields block) as a blue band between warm ones. */
 body.page-id-150{background:#FAF8F4}
 /* ⚠️ THE HEADLINE NEVER WAS SERIF. leonardo-homepage-css.min.css carries
 `.lh-wrap .lh-title{font-family:system-ui !important; font-size:44px
 !important; font-weight:800 !important; color:#003b73 !important}`, so
 the Source Serif rule earlier in this block lost on every device. Only
 !important with equal-or-higher specificity can beat it. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}

 EUROPE") already does that job; the extra pill only added noise. */
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{display:none}

 the screen edge while the centred text did not. Left-aligned, with the
 same 20px gutter as the rest of the page, it matches the desktop. */
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{padding-left:20px;padding-right:20px;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:left}

 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title{text-align:left}

 }

 Serif headings and a small monospaced label instead of the rounded blue
 pills, which were the last "app" element on the page. */

 .lh-wrap .lh-section-badge{display:inline-block;margin-bottom:14px;padding:0;background:none;border-radius:0;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;font-weight:500;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#8C5A23}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-sub{color:#4A525C}
 /* Section rhythm: paper / white / paper, so each block has an edge. */

 .lh-wrap .lh-unis{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}

 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px}
 /* ── Study fields block (rendered by [sie_study_fields] after .lh-wrap) ─
 Six bright category colours, gradient pills and a gradient CTA made it

 The branch colours arrive as INLINE custom properties and inline
 backgrounds, so these overrides need !important to apply. Scoped to the
 homepage: the study-field pages keep their colour coding. */
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-weight:600;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px);letter-spacing:-.4px;color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-subtitle{color:#4A525C}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__junction-dot{background:#12233D}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-count{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-icon{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__leo-link{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leonardo{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:6px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leo-btn{background:#fff !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#fff !important;border-radius:4px}
 /* Alignment: the search widget carries its own 24px side padding, so the
 bar sat indented from the headline above it; and the trust row was
 centred under a left-aligned column. Both now share the text's edge.
 Only the LEFT padding goes: removing the right one too pushed the
 "AI-enhanced matching" toggle across the seam into the navy side. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-wrap{padding-left:0 !important}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 /* Institution cards: the stylesheet tints each card top a different pastel

 monogram or logo is the only thing that differs between cards. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card:nth-child(n) .lh-uni-card-top{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border-bottom:1px solid #EDEAE3}
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-cta{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 .lh-wrap .sie-dest-hub__name{color:#12233D}
 /* Europe silhouette on the navy side. Present, never loud: a lighter blue

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">Conference on the Future of Europe : the future is in your hands</h1>
<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs.                                                 <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility.         <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">During the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q10.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> During the mobility, your institution fosters the integration of the incoming mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution appoints responsible person(s) to deal with practical issues (e.g. social, health, and/or psychological problems)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should ensure there are named, visible persons who are responsible for the practical issues associated with integrating mobile students. This visibility should be ensured through introduction to this function during the Welcome / Orientation period and be detailed on the website so all mobile students can easily access this support, throughout their stay.&nbsp;</p><p>Non-academic mentoring and support arrangements should already be outlined in the Course Catalogue of the receiving HEI, in the section on general information for students, with relevant contact persons in the respective areas. Academic advisors should have close contact with the practical services which are available to incoming participants as they are often the first line of contact to the incoming student. Further information sessions should be arranged for all staff who work with incoming students to ensure they are adequately signposted on to the appropriate services they require.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It appoints responsible person(s) to deal with academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important that the receiving institution appoints specific named academic advisors who are responsible for dealing with problems related to academic issues (course timetables, student attendance, coursework, relationship with academic staff, etc.) of incoming students.&nbsp; Information on mentoring for thesis writing for incoming students is particularly important and clear mentoring arrangements should be agreed upon between the student, sending and receiving institutions and organised before the mobility.</p><p>For traineeships, a mentor, different from the supervisor, should be nominated to support and encourage the mobile student while in the receiving organisation. The mentor should also provide information on the culture of the enterprise and informal codes and conducts, of the receiving organisation. The contact details of both the supervisor and the mentor should be specified in the Learning Agreement.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It organises Welcome / Orientation activities at the beginning of each semester</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>An important aspect of the support arrangement is the welcome or orientation activities. These welcome / orientation activities should provide the incoming students with the necessary information on practical and administrative arrangements, to allow incoming students to meet local and other mobile students, to introduce the learning and teaching methods of the receiving institution, academic regulations, the institutional culture, health and safety issues. These activities should address any type of concern of the incoming student, and reduce any psychological pressure they might feel during their first contacts at the receiving institution. The welcome&nbsp; / orientation activities should be designed to take into account any cultural and religious sensitivities of the incoming students (ensuring a range of activities to suit different types of students).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It organises activities to integrate them in the receiving institution and the local community, e.g. with the support of student organisations, Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association etc.</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>As well as academic and practical support from the institution, incoming students need to feel fully integrated into the student community, something which is best done by their fellow students / peers. Local student association(s), such as Erasmus Student Network (ESN) and the other associations’ member of the ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>), play an important role in supporting incoming students. Incoming students need to feel welcomed and included in the student organisations. To help this process, the student organisations need to be aware of their role in supporting this integration and have access to the right resources, information, guidance and incentives. As institutions often have many types of student organisations, cooperation between them is encouraged through meetings together, social activities and buddy programmes. A key aspect of these activities is to make sure they are for all students so incoming students are integrated with the local students and hence the culture. Student organisations include for example, ESN (Erasmus Student Network) or ESAA - Erasmus+ Student and Alumni Association (<a href="http://esaa-eu.org/">http://esaa-eu.org/</a>). ESAA runs a buddy system to encourage integration of incoming students with their peers inside the institution and share good practice with other member associations around Europe.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides opportunities for incoming mobile participants to share their culture and experiences with their peers inside and with the local community</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Incoming mobile students also bring new perspectives to the institution, the local students and the culture which is part of the internationalisation of the receiving institution. This is a significant opportunity to benefit from the experiences that international students bring. To capitalise on these experiences, the institution and its student organisations should put in place opportunities for incoming students to showcase their talent and perspectives through access to existing local initiatives (e.g. school teaching programmes, community projects) and setting up new initiatives to celebrate the different cultures (e.g. theatre performances, food and cultural weeks etc.). Local associations can support the integration of incoming students with the local community, through existing initiatives such as the Social Erasmus and Erasmus in School projects (<a href="http://socialerasmus.esn.org">http://socialerasmus.esn.org</a>).&nbsp;</p><p>Some incoming students may even have been involved in the management or governance of their sending institutions and recognising this opportunity and involving incoming students in similar functions in the receiving institution such as in the student union (elected representative) or working groups dedicated to the voice of the international student.&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>                      </div>

        <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">After the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">
                <div class="eche-officer-question-title-wrapper">
                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">
                            <img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/eche-pdf/number-corner-orange-11.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">11</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q11.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
